radiologic features reliably distinguish between typical bacterial, atypical bacterial, and viral pneumonia. (See <u>'Bacterial versus viral etiology'</u> above and <u>"Pneumonia in children: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and etiology"</u>, section on '<u>Etiologic agents</u>'.))

Testing for critical microbes is indicated if there is a local outbreak. (See <u>'Critical microbes'</u> below.)

**Chest imaging** â€” Chest imaging typically consists of radiographs. Bedside lung ultrasonography has been used to detect lung consolidation in pediatric emergency and inpatient settings [71-75]. However, diagnostic accuracy appears to be affected by the level of experience of the sonographer [76].

- **Views** â€“ Radiographic views depend upon the age of the child [77]. In children older than four years, the frontal posteroanterior (PA) upright chest view is usually obtained to minimize the size of the cardiac shadow [78]. In younger children, the anteroposterior (AP) supine view is preferred because the child's position does not affect the size of the cardiothoracic shadow in this age group and immobilization is easier, improving the likelihood of an adequate inspiration [78].

There is a lack of consensus regarding the need for lateral views to demonstrate infiltrates that may be obscured by the dome of the diaphragm or the cardiac shadow on AP or PA views [<u>1,2,55,79</u>]. In a review of chest radiographs in 201 children with pneumonia, the lateral film was abnormal in 91 percent of 109 children with definite pneumonia [80]. However, the AP or PA views also demonstrated pneumonia in all but three cases. A lateral view may be more valuable in settings where the radiographs are interpreted by nonradiologists.

Of note, the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society and Infectious Diseases Society of America suggest PA and lateral views for all children who are hospitalized for management of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) [1].

A lateral decubitus view (with the affected side down) may be needed to identify a pleural effusion. (See <u>"Epidemiology, clinical presentation, and evaluation of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children"</u>, section on '<u>Radiologic evaluation</u>'.))

- **Findings** â€“ Radiographic features do not reliably differentiate between typical bacterial, atypical bacterial, and viral pneumonia [8,81-83] and should be used in conjunction with clinical findings to make therapeutic decisions (ðŸ“Š table 2) [<u>2,84-87</u>].

In children with viral pneumonia, interstitial infiltrates are the primary radiographic finding.

Radiographic features that are more often associated with a bacterial etiology include:

- Segmental and lobar consolidation â€“ Segmental and lobar consolidation are reasonably specific for bacterial pneumonia but lack sensitivity [86,88-90]. These findings are the most common ones associated with *M. pneumoniae* (37 percent) [91]. Radiologic features of

- Pulmonary consolidation â€“ Pulmonary consolidation in young children sometimes appears to be spherical (ie, "round pneumonia") (<u>image 4</u>) [<u>94,95</u>]. Round pneumonias tend to be >3 cm, solitary, and posteriorly located [<u>95,96</u>]. *S. pneumoniae* is the most common bacterial etiology of round pneumonia; additional bacterial causes include other streptococci, *H. influenzae*, *S. aureus*, and *M. pneumoniae* [<u>86,97</u>].

- Peribronchial infiltrates â€“ Peribronchial infiltrates are suggestive of *M. pneumoniae* pneumonia (27 percent) (<u>image 5</u>) [<u>91</u>]. However, *S. pneumoniae* has occasionally been associated with peribronchial infiltrates in children.

- Hyperinflation with interstitial infiltrates â€“ Hyperinflation with interstitial infiltrates is characteristic of afebrile pneumonia of infancy typically caused by *C. trachomatis*. (See "<u>Chlamydia trachomatis infections in newborns and young infants</u>", section on 'Pneumonia'.)

- Pneumatoceles, cavitations, large pleural effusions, and necrotizing processes â€“ Complications of pneumonia (eg, pneumatoceles, cavitations, large pleural effusions (<u>image 2A</u> and <u>image 2B</u>), necrotizing processes (<u>image 3</u>) suggest a typical bacterial etiology (eg, *S. pneumoniae*, *S. aureus*, *Streptococcus pyogenes*) and, rarely, *M. pneumoniae*. ## **Microbiologic testing** â€” Our approach to microbiologic testing is generally consistent with that of the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society and the Infectious Diseases Society of America clinical practice guidelines [<u>1</u>]. (See '<u>Society guideline links</u>' below.)

## **Blood cultures** â€” We obtain blood cultures in children who require hospitalization because they are more likely to have bacteremia than those who are treated in the outpatient setting. (See "<u>Detection of bacteremia: Blood cultures and other diagnostic tests</u>".)

Observational studies conducted in the postpneumococcal conjugate vaccine era demonstrate prevalences of bacteremic pneumonia ranging from 2.2 to 7 percent in hospitalized children who had blood cultures obtained [<u>104-106</u>]. In a prospective study, blood cultures were obtained in 91 percent of 2358 children who were hospitalized with radiographically confirmed pneumonia and were positive in 2.2 percent (95% CI 1.6-2.9 percent) [<u>106</u>]. Most isolates were susceptible to penicillin. *S. pneumoniae* (46 percent), *S. aureus* (6 percent), and *S. pyogenes* (9 percent) were the most frequently isolated pathogens. In this and other observational studies, the prevalence of bacteremia was increased in patients with complicated pneumonia or pneumonia-related metastatic complications (eg, osteomyelitis) [<u>104-110</u>].

Targeting blood cultures to children who are at increased risk for bacteremia (eg, those with pleural effusion/empyema, admission to the intensive care unit, or immunosuppression) may be clinically effective and reduce costs [<u>110,111</u>]. However, determining which children are at risk for bacteremia at the time of admission can be difficult. In one multicenter study, 6 of the 26 patients with bacteremia were initially thought to have uncomplicated pneumonia [<u>104</u>].

## **Sputum Gram stain and culture** â€” We obtain sputum samples for Gram stain and culture in children who require hospital admission if they are able to produce sputum [<u>1</u>]. Children younger than five years usually swallow sputum, so it is rarely available for examination.

Although good-quality sputum samples can be obtained by sputum induction [<u>112,113</u>], sputum induction is unpleasant. In addition, in a prospective study of the etiology of pneumonia in hospitalized children <18 years of age, bacterial pathogens were isolated from most induced sputum cultures regardless of sputum quality or whether the child had radiographically confirmed pneumonia, suggesting identification of oropharyngeal carriage rather than the pathogenic etiology of the pneumonia [<u>113</u>].

An aggressive approach to determining a definitive microbial diagnosis is necessary for immunocompromised patients with pneumonia that requires hospitalization. Invasive procedures may be required to obtain a satisfactory specimen. For patients with an

## **Pleural fluid Gram stain and culture** â€” Diagnostic (and possibly therapeutic) thoracentesis is generally warranted for children with more than minimal pleural effusion identified on radiographs. Specimens for culture should ideally be obtained before administration of antibiotics. If patients receive antibiotics before a pleural effusion is identified, molecular testing of the fluid for detection of *S. pneumoniae*, *S. pyogenes*, and *S. aureus* using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) techniques (when available) may be warranted. The evaluation of pleural fluid is discussed separately. (See "Epidemiology, clinical presentation, and evaluation of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children", section on 'Pleural fluid analysis'.)

## **Rapid diagnostic testing** â€” When available, we prefer rapid diagnostic tests to cultures because the results are available much sooner. Results of rapid diagnostic tests can be helpful in making treatment and/or cohorting decisions for infants and children who are admitted to the hospital with probable CAP, regardless of the suspected etiology [1,114]. Importantly, rapid viral testing cannot be used in isolation to exclude bacterial infection because patients, particularly those who are severely ill, may have a concomitant bacterial-viral infection [115].

Rapid diagnostic testing for respiratory viruses is usually done by real-time (RT) PCR. Multiplex RT-PCR viral panels can detect respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza A and B, SARS-CoV-2, and other common respiratory viruses. These tests are performed on nasopharyngeal (NP) swabs, and results are typically available within a few hours. They can also be performed on pleural fluid. Immunofluorescence antigen tests are also available but are less sensitive than PCR.

Additionally, PCR tests are available for the detection of *S. pneumoniae* (performed on sputum, pleural fluid, and abscess contents) and *M. pneumoniae* (performed on a throat swab) [116]. In prospective studies, qualitative PCR of respiratory samples had a higher yield than culture for identification of *S. pneumoniae* [3,117,118]. However, this may merely represent respiratory tract colonization. *S. pneumoniae* PCR testing of pleural fluid or abscess contents, on the other hand, may help to differentiate colonization from infection [119-121].

*M. pneumoniae* PCR testing can be helpful in evaluating the younger child (ie, <4 years) with consistent symptoms given that *M. pneumoniae* is less common in children <4 years of age. PCR testing may also help to establish the diagnosis in patients with extrapulmonary manifestations of *M. pneumoniae*, particularly central nervous system manifestations [15]. (See "Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection in children", section on 'Clinical manifestations'.)

## **Less commonly used tests** â€” Other tests that may be helpful in establishing less common microbiologic etiologies of CAP in children with appropriate clinical indications include:

- Interferon gamma release assay and tuberculin skin test â€“ If pulmonary tuberculosis is a consideration, a serum interferon gamma release assay or a tuberculin skin test is warranted. Indications include exposure to an individual with active tuberculosis (ðŸ“‹ table 9), being foreign born, having a foreign-born caregiver, a history of foreign travel, and exposure to an individual who traveled to an endemic area. Additional diagnostic testing for tuberculosis in children is discussed separately. (See "Tuberculosis disease (active tuberculosis) in children: Epidemiology, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis".))

- Urine antigen testing for legionellosis due to serogroup 1 â€“ If *Legionella* is a consideration (eg, pneumonia in an immunocompromised host; known/suspected outbreak in a building, cruise ship, etc), urine antigen testing for legionellosis due to serogroup 1 is recommended. Diagnosis of *Legionella* infection is discussed in detail separately. (See "Clinical manifestations and diagnosis of Legionella infection", section on 'Approach to testing' and "Microbiology, epidemiology, and pathogenesis of Legionella infection", section on 'Pathogen'.))

- Serum and urine antigen and antibody testing for histoplasmosis â€“ If histoplasmosis is a consideration, serum and urine antigen and antibody testing should be conducted (ie,

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/community-acquired-pneumonia-in-children-clinical-features-and-diagnosis/print?search=pneumonia&sourc... 16/52

3/18/26, 5:09 PM Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis - UpToDate

complement fixation, immunodiffusion, and enzyme immunoassay [EIA] immunoglobulin M [IgM]/immunoglobulin G [IgG]). Indications for testing include exposure to soil contaminated with bird droppings or bat guano in an endemic area <u>[122]</u>. Diagnostic testing for histoplasmosis is discussed in more detail separately. (See "<u>Pathogenesis and clinical features of pulmonary histoplasmosis</u>" and "<u>Diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary histoplasmosis</u>", section on 'Antigen detection'.)

Urine antigen testing for *S. pneumoniae* in children should **not be** performed because of concern for false-positive reactions, some of which may merely indicate colonization with *S. pneumoniae* <u>[1,2]</u>; additional studies are needed to evaluate the potential usefulness of this diagnostic technique in children with and without CAP <u>[123]</u>.

We do not suggest routine serologic testing for specific pathogens (eg, *S. pneumoniae*, *M. pneumoniae*, *C. pneumoniae*) because the results usually do not influence management <u>[124,125]</u>. *S. pneumoniae* has too many potential infecting serotypes to make antibody determinations practical. IgM antibody testing for *M. pneumoniae* may give false-positive results. Serologic tests for *Chlamydia* spp are not readily available. Serologic diagnosis of viral pathogens is not practical because acute and convalescent specimens are needed.

We do not obtain NP cultures for etiologic diagnosis in children with pneumonia. Bacterial organisms cultured from the nasopharynx may be normal upper respiratory flora. Although the results of NP cultures for viruses and atypical bacteria may be helpful, they may not be available soon enough to assist with management decisions.

The addition of cell-free plasma sequencing and transcriptional profile analysis to diagnostic capabilities awaits the results of further studies in children with CAP and more widespread availability <u>[126,127]</u>. These laboratory approaches may be most useful in immunocompromised hosts with CAP for whom the risks of invasive procedures may outweigh the benefits <u>[128]</u>.

**Critical microbes** â€” Diagnostic testing for an unusual pathogen (critical microbe) should be conducted if the patient has characteristic symptoms, a close contact, or if there is an outbreak. These pathogens require treatment that differs from standard empiric regimens for CAP and have public health implications.

- Fungal etiologies (*Coccidioides immitis*, *Blastomyces dermatitidis*, *Histoplasma capsulatum*) (see "<u>Primary pulmonary coccidioidal infection</u>" and "<u>Mycology, pathogenesis, and epidemiology</u>"

## **INFORMATION FOR PATIENTS**

UpToDate offers two types of patient education materials, "The Basics" and "Beyond the Basics." The Basics patient education pieces are written in plain language, at the <sup>5<sup>th</sup></sup> to <sup>6<sup>th</sup></sup> grade reading level, and they answer the four or five key questions a patient might have about a given condition. These articles are best for patients who want a general overview and who prefer short, easy-to-read materials. Beyond the Basics patient education pieces are longer, more sophisticated, and more detailed. These articles are written at the <sup>10<sup>th</sup></sup> to <sup>12<sup>th</sup></sup> grade reading level and are best for patients who want in-depth information and are comfortable with some medical jargon.

Here are the patient education articles that are relevant to this topic. We encourage you to print or email these topics to your patients. (You can also locate patient education articles on a variety of subjects by searching on "patient education" and the keyword[s] of interest.)

## **SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS**

- **Clinical presentation**

- **Clinical features** â€“ Children with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) typically have a combination of fever and cough and possibly other respiratory findings (eg, tachypnea, increased work of breathing), depending on the severity of the infection. Additional signs and symptoms vary by age. (See 'Clinical features' above.)

- **Etiology (bacterial versus viral)** â€“ Clinical features that are traditionally considered characteristic of typical bacterial pneumonia, atypical bacterial pneumonia, and viral pneumonia frequently overlap and cannot be used reliably to distinguish between the

- **Objectives** â€“ The clinical evaluation should focus on features that help to define the clinical syndrome (eg, pneumonia, bronchiolitis) and determine the likely etiology (eg, bacteria, virus) (<u>table 2</u>). (See 'Objectives' above and "<u>Pneumonia in children: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and etiology</u>", section on 'Etiologic agents'.)

various etiologies. As many as 50 percent of infections are mixed bacterial-viral infections. However, features that are typically seen with each type of pneumonia can help to make a clinical diagnosis (<u>table 2</u>). (See '<u>Bacterial versus viral etiology</u>' above.)

- **Clinical evaluation**

- **History** â€“ Historical features help determine the presumptive microbiologic etiology (<u>table 3</u> and <u>table 4</u>), the likelihood of infection with an organism that is resistant to antibiotics, and the risk of a missed foreign body or anatomical abnormality. (See '<u>History</u>' above.)
  - **Physical examination** â€“ Important aspects of the physical examination include general appearance (eg, state of awareness), temperature (eg, afebrile, fever â‰¥39Â°C), degree of respiratory distress, and lung examination (<u>table 6</u>). (See '<u>Physical examination</u>' above.)
  - **Radiologic evaluation** â€“ Radiographs are not necessary for children with mild pneumonia who are well enough to be treated as outpatients unless there is a history of recurrent pneumonia. Recurrent pneumonia may indicate a missed foreign body or anatomical abnormality. (See '<u>Radiographs</u>' above.)
  - **Establishing the diagnosis** â€“ The diagnosis of pneumonia is established in a child who has fever and cough, evidence by history or on physical examination of an infectious pulmonary process (<u>table 3</u> and <u>table 6</u>), and symptoms or signs of respiratory distress. (See '<u>Establishing the diagnosis</u>' above.)

Although no single symptom or sign is pathognomonic for pneumonia in children, the longer that fever, cough, and respiratory findings are present, the greater the likelihood of pneumonia.

- **Assessing severity** â€“ The history and physical examination are used to assess the severity of illness (<u>table 5</u>), which determines, in part, whether hospitalization is indicated. (See '<u>Assessing severity</u>' above.)
  - **Differential diagnosis** â€“ The differential diagnosis includes common respiratory illnesses (eg, upper respiratory tract infection with cough, bronchiolitis, asthma, comorbid asthma with viral respiratory infection) and less common diagnoses (eg, foreign body aspiration, vaping-associated pulmonary illness, other causes of tachypnea, and noninfectious mimics of pneumonia) (<u>table 7</u>). (See '<u>Differential diagnosis</u>' above.)

- **Complications** â€“ Complications of CAP in children include pleural effusion and empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, lung abscess, pneumatocele, and hyponatremia. (See '<u>Complications</u>' above.)

- **Indications for additional diagnostic testing** â€“ Most children with mild pneumonia who are well enough to be treated as outpatients do not require additional diagnostic testing. # GRAPHICS

## Table 1: Pneumonia terminology

| Term                                               | Definition                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Classification by site of acquisition**          |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)                 | An acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma acquired outside of health care settings                                                                                                                                                     |
| Nosocomial pneumonia                               | An acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma acquired in hospital settings, which encompasses hospital-acquired pneumonia and ventilator-associated pneumonia                                                                             |
| Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP)                  | Pneumonia acquired â‰¥48 hours after hospital admission; includes both HAP and VAP                                                                                                                                                            |
| Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)              | Pneumonia acquired â‰¥48 hours after endotracheal intubation                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Non-ventilated hospital-acquired pneumonia (nvHAP) | Pneumonia that develops in hospitalized patients who are not on mechanical ventilation nor underwent extubation within 48 hours before pneumonia developed                                                                                  |
| Health care-associated pneumonia (HCAP)            | Retired term, which referred to pneumonia acquired in health care facilities (eg, nursing homes, hemodialysis centers) or after recent hospitalization\*                                                                                    |
| **Classification by etiology**                     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Atypical pneumonia                                 | Pneumonia caused by "atypical"â€¡ pathogens including *Legionella spp*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia psittaci*, *Coxiella burnetii*                                                                            |
| Aspiration pneumonia                               | Pneumonia resulting from entry of gastric or oropharyngeal fluid, which may contain bacteria and/or exogenous substances (eg, ingested food particles or liquids, mineral oil, salt or fresh water) or be of low pH, into the lower airways |
| Chemical pneumonitis                               | Aspiration of substances (eg, acidic gastric fluid) that cause an inflammatory reaction in the lower airways, independent of bacterial infection                                                                                            |
| Bacterial aspiration pneumonia                     | An active infection caused by inoculation of large amounts of bacteria into the lungs via orogastric contents                                                                                                                               |

* The term HCAP was used to identify patients at risk for infection with multidrug-resistant pathogens. This categorization may have been overly sensitive, leading to increased, inappropriately broad antibiotic use.

â€¡ The origin of the term "atypical" is a matter of debate. The term may refer to the fact that these organisms are not "typical" bacteria (eg, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*), which can be identified by standard microbiologic techniques. Others suggest that atypical refers to the mild nature of the pneumonia caused by some of these organisms compared with pneumonia caused by *S. pneumoniae*.

# Table 2: Clinical and radiographic clues to the etiology of pneumonia in children

| Etiology                                                              | Clinical features                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Radiographic features                                                                                                                                                                              |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Bacterial (most commonly *Streptococcus pneumoniae*)                  | - Children of all ages - Abrupt onset - Ill appearance - Chills - Moderate to severe respiratory distress - Focal auscultatory findings - Localized chest pain - WBC count >15,000/mL (if obtained) - Elevated acute phase reactants (if obtained)                                                                                                                                                                    | - Alveolar infiltrates - Segmental consolidation - Lobar consolidation - "Round" pneumonia \*\*Complications:\*\* - Pleural effusion/empyema - Lung abscess - Necrotizing pneumonia - Pneumatocele |
| Atypical bacterial (most commonly *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*)            | - Children of all ages (most common in children >5 years) - Abrupt onset with gradually worsening constitutional findings (malaise, myalgia, headache, rash, conjunctivitis, photophobia, sore throat) and nonproductive cough - Wheezing - Extrapulmonary manifestations or complications (eg, polymorphous mucocutaneous eruptions, hemolytic anemia, hepatitis, pancreatitis, myopericarditis, aseptic meningitis) | - Lobar or segmental consolidation (37%) - Perihilar or peribronchial infiltrates (27%) - Localized reticulonodular infiltrates (21%) - Patchy infiltrates (15%)                                   |
| Viral                                                                 | - Usually children <5 years - Gradual onset - Preceding upper airway symptoms - Nontoxic appearance - Diffuse, bilateral auscultatory findings - Wheezing - May have associated rash (eg, measles, varicella)                                                                                                                                                                                                         | - Interstitial infiltrates - \*\*Associated bronchiolitis:\*\* - Patchy atelectasis - Peribronchial infiltrations with air bronchograms - Hyperinflation with flattening of the diaphragms         |
| Afebrile pneumonia of infancy (most commonly *Chlamydia trachomatis*) | - Usually in infants 1 to 3 months of age - Insidious onset - Tachypnea, diffuse crackles - Rhinorrhea - Staccato cough pattern - Peripheral eosinophilia (if CBC obtained)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | - Hyperinflation with interstitial infiltrates                                                                                                                                                     |

* The clinical features frequently overlap and cannot reliably distinguish between bacterial, atypical bacterial, and viral etiologies; up to one-half of community-acquired pneumonias in children may be mixed bacterial/viral infections. Chest radiography generally is not helpful in determining the potential causative agent of pneumonia. Nonetheless, these features may facilitate decisions regarding empiric therapy.

# **Image 1: Pneumococcal pneumonia: Complications**

Radiographic images of the complications of pneumococcal pneumonia.
**(Left panel)** Lung abscess with an air-fluid level in the right lung. Abscess cavity material is nearly always culture positive, and patients commonly defervesce within 48 hours of interventional drainage.
**(Right panel)** Radiograph of necrotizing pneumonia in the left lung.

# Picture 2: **Primary varicella lesions**

Primary varicella lesions

Vesicular lesions on an erythematous base are characteristic of chickenpox. The lesions occur in crops and are present in a variety of stages from maculopapular to vesicular or even pustular. Central necrosis and early crusting is also visible.

# Table 3: **Important aspects of the history in a child with pneumonia**

| Historical feature                                                            | Possible significance                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Age of the child                                                              | Viral etiologies are most common in infants and preschool children<br/>Atypical bacterial pathogens are more common in school-age children                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Recent viral upper respiratory tract infection                                | May predispose to bacterial superinfection with *Streptococcus pneumoniae* or *Staphylococcus aureus*                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Associated symptoms                                                           | *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* is often associated with extrapulmonary manifestations (eg, headache, sore throat, conjunctivitis, photophobia, rash)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing                  | "Classic" features of pneumonia, but nonspecific                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Increased work of breathing in the absence of stridor or wheezing             | Suggestive of more severe pneumonia                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Fluid and nutrition intake                                                    | Difficulty or inability to feed suggests severe illness                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Choking episode                                                               | May indicate foreign body aspiration                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Duration of symptoms                                                          | Chronic cough (>4 weeks) suggests etiology other than acute pneumonia (refer to UpToDate topic on causes of chronic cough in children)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Previous episodes                                                             | Recurrent episodes may indicate aspiration, congenital or acquired anatomic abnormality, cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency, asthma, missed foreign body                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Immunization status                                                           | Completion of the primary series of immunizations for *Haemophilus influenzae* type b, *S. pneumoniae*, *Bordetella pertussis*, and seasonal influenza decreases, but does not eliminate, the risk of infection with these organisms                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Previous antibiotic therapy                                                   | Increases the likelihood of antibiotic-resistant bacteria                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Maternal history of chlamydia during pregnancy (for infants <4 months of age) | May indicate *Chlamydia trachomatis* infection                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Foreign travel or known exposure to tuberculosis                              | May indicate *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* infection                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Ill contacts                                                                  | More common with viral etiologies                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Travel to or residence in certain areas that suggest endemic pathogens        | - Measles: Resource-limited countries - Coccidioidomycosis: Southwestern United States, northern Mexico, Central and South America - Blastomycosis: Southeastern and Central United States; states bordering the Great Lakes - Histoplasmosis: Ohio, Missouri, and Mississippi River valleys in the United States; Canada; Central America; eastern and southern Europe; parts of Africa; eastern Asia; and Australia |

# Table 5: Severity of community-acquired pneumonia in infants and children

| **Clinical features of mild pneumonia (all of the following)**                                                                                                                       | **Clinical features of severe pneumonia (1 or more of the following)**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mild or absent respiratory distress:- â–  No to mild tachypnea for age\*
- â–  Mild or absent retractions
- â–  No grunting
- â–  No nasal flaring
- â–  No apnea
- â–  Mild shortness of breath | Severe respiratory distress:- â–  RR >70 breaths/minute for infants; RR >50 breaths/minute for older children
- â–  Severe suprasternal, intercostal, or subcostal retractions (<12 months)
- â–  Severe difficulty breathing (â‰¥12 months)
- â–  Grunting
- â–  Nasal flaring
- â–  Apnea
- â–  Significant shortness of breath |

RR: respiratory rate.

# **Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis**

**AUTHOR:** William J Barson, MD
**SECTION EDITOR:** Sheldon L Kaplan, MD
**DEPUTY EDITOR:** Diane Blake, MD

All topics are updated as new evidence becomes available and our peer review process is complete.

Literature review current through: **Feb 2026.**
This topic last updated: **Oct 30, 2025.**

## INTRODUCTION

Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is defined by signs and symptoms of an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma in an individual who acquired the infection in the community, as distinguished from hospital-acquired (nosocomial) pneumonia (<u>table 1</u>) [1,2]. CAP is a common and potentially serious illness with considerable morbidity. Mild pneumonia is sometimes referred to as "walking pneumonia" because the symptoms do not interfere with normal activity.

The clinical features and diagnosis of CAP in children will be reviewed here. The epidemiology, pathogenesis, and treatment of pneumonia in children are discussed separately.

- (See "Pneumonia in children: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and etiology".)
- (See "Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Outpatient treatment".)
- (See "Pneumonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment".)

## CLINICAL PRESENTATION

### Clinical features

- **Features common to all ages** â€“ Children with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) typically have a combination of fever and cough and possibly other respiratory findings (eg, tachypnea, increased work of breathing), depending on the severity of the infection. Cough is triggered by the products of infection, which irritate cough receptors in the airways. In one study of children hospitalized for radiographically confirmed pneumonia, 95 percent had cough, 90 percent had fever, 75 percent had anorexia, 70 percent had dyspnea, and 55 percent had chest

**Bacterial versus viral etiology** â€” The features that are traditionally considered characteristic of typical bacterial pneumonia, atypical bacterial pneumonia, and viral pneumonia (<u>table 2</u>) frequently overlap and cannot be used reliably to distinguish between the various etiologies [8,9]. In addition, as many as 50 percent of infections are mixed bacterial/viral infections. (See <u>"Pneumonia in children: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and etiology", section on 'Community-acquired pneumonia'</u>.)

wall retraits [3]. Although no single symptom or sign is pathognomonic for pneumonia in children, the longer that fever, cough, and respiratory findings are present, the greater the likelihood of pneumonia <u>[4,5]</u>.

- **Infants and young children** â€“ Young infants may present with difficulty feeding, restlessness, or fussiness rather than with cough and/or abnormal breath sounds [6]. Symptoms and signs of pneumonia may be subtle. Infants and young children may present with only fever and leukocytosis [5,7]. The clinical features of neonatal pneumonia are discussed separately. (See <u>"Neonatal pneumonia", section on 'Clinical presentation'</u>.)

- **Older children and adolescents** â€“ Older children and adolescents may experience pleuritic chest pain (pain with respiration), but this is an inconsistent finding [4]. Occasionally, the predominant manifestation in older children and adolescents is abdominal pain (because of referred pain from the lower lobes) or nuchal rigidity (because of referred pain from the upper lobes).

Nevertheless, the diagnosis of bacterial versus atypical bacterial versus viral CAP is generally made clinically, and the following features are typically seen with each pneumonia category:

- **Bacterial** â€“ Children with "typical" bacterial pneumonia tend to have an abrupt onset of symptoms (eg, fever, chills, cough, focal chest pain), which may be preceded by days of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms. Febrile patients usually appear ill and sometimes toxic. Respiratory distress may be moderate to severe; auscultatory findings may be few and focal, limited to the involved anatomic segment.

Pneumococcal pneumonia is the most common cause of typical bacterial pneumonia in children of all ages. Pneumonia due to *Haemophilus influenzae* type b (Hib) may still occur in areas with low Hib conjugate vaccine uptake. Typable non-type b and nontypable *H. influenzae* are uncommon causes of childhood pneumonia. Typical bacterial pneumonia is less commonly caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* and group A *Streptococcus*. Fever and cough occur in the majority of children with typical bacterial pneumonia. Other common findings include malaise/lethargy, decreased breath sounds, and crackles. Pneumococcal pneumonia in children is discussed in greater detail separately. (See <u>"Pneumococcal pneumonia in children"</u>.)

In patients with severe illness, signs and symptoms of sepsis and localized chest pain (signifying pleural irritation) are more suggestive of a bacterial etiology because they are

3/18/26, 5:09 PM Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis - UpToDate
- **Viral** â€“ The onset of viral pneumonia is gradual and associated with preceding upper respiratory tract symptoms (eg, rhinorrhea, congestion). The child does not typically appear toxic. Auscultatory findings are usually diffuse and bilateral. In one study of 98 ambulatory children with pneumonia, wheezing was more frequent in patients with viral than bacterial pneumonia (43 versus 16 percent), but other clinical features often associated with viral illness (such as rhinorrhea, myalgia, and ill contacts) were not [17].

rarely present in nonbacterial pneumonia [10]. Complications of pneumonia are also more suggestive of bacterial etiology (<u>image 1</u>). (See 'Complications' below.)

- **Atypical bacterial** â€“ "Atypical" bacterial pneumonia usually presents abruptly with constitutional findings (eg, fever, malaise, myalgia, headache, photophobia, sore throat, conjunctivitis, rash) that gradually worsen. These are followed by a nonproductive cough that gradually worsens even as the other symptoms improve [11,12]. Wheezing is a frequent finding in atypical bacterial pneumonia [10].

*Mycoplasma pneumoniae* or *Chlamydia pneumoniae* are the usual causes of atypical bacterial pneumonia. *M. pneumoniae* is the most common cause of bacterial pneumonia in otherwise healthy children â‰¥5 years of age [13]. Although hoarseness may be seen in disease caused by both pathogens, it is more frequently seen with *C. pneumoniae* infection. (See "<u>Pneumonia caused by Chlamydia pneumoniae in children</u>" and "<u>*Mycoplasma pneumoniae* infection in children</u>", section on 'Clinical manifestations'.)

*M. pneumoniae* may be associated with a variety of extrapulmonary manifestations. Dermatologic manifestations may range from a mild erythematous maculopapular rash or urticaria to *M. pneumoniae*-induced rash and mucositis (MIRM) and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Other extrapulmonary manifestations include hemolytic anemia, polyarthritits, pancreatitis, hepatitis, pericarditis, myocarditis, and neurologic complications [14,15]. (See "<u>*Mycoplasma pneumoniae* infection in children</u>", section on 'Clinical manifestations'.)

Young infants may develop "afebrile pneumonia of infancy." Afebrile pneumonia of infancy is a syndrome generally seen between one to three months of age, but it can occur as early as two weeks or as late as four months of age. It is classically caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*, but other agents (such as cytomegalovirus, *Mycoplasma hominis*, and *Ureaplasma urealyticum*) are also implicated. The clinical presentation is one of insidious onset of rhinorrhea and tachypnea followed by a staccato cough pattern (individual coughs separated by inspirations). Physical examination typically reveals diffuse inspiratory crackles. Conjunctivitis may be present, or there may have been a past history of conjunctivitis [16]. (See "<u>Chlamydia trachomatis infections in newborns and young infants</u>", section on 'Pneumonia'.)

In children younger than two years of age, >80 percent of CAP infections are caused by viruses [3].

## **Clinical course**

- **Typical and atypical bacterial pneumonia** â€“ Children who are appropriately treated for CAP generally show signs of improvement within 48 to 72 hours and continue to gradually improve with time. They may continue to have a residual cough for several weeks and have moderate dyspnea on exertion for two to three months.

- **Viral pneumonia** â€“ Children with viral pneumonia generally show signs of improvement within three to seven days, with full resolution of their symptoms by one month. Rarely, the cough may last for several weeks depending on the causative agent (eg, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 [SARS-CoV-2]).

## **CLINICAL EVALUATION**

### **Initial evaluation for all patients**

**Objectives** â€” Goals of the initial evaluation include: identifying the clinical syndrome (eg, pneumonia versus bronchiolitis or asthma); determining the likely etiology (eg, bacteria, virus) (<img> table 2); and assessing the severity of the illness [6]. The severity of illness helps determine whether hospitalization is indicated.

**History** â€” Important aspects of the history in children with possible community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) include age of the child, details about the presenting symptoms, and a previous history of pneumonia or antibiotic use. These and other aspects of the history are outlined in the table (<img> table 3) [4,18]. Historical features may help determine the presumptive microbiologic etiology (<img> table 4), the likelihood of infection with an organism that is resistant to antibiotics, the risk of a missed foreign body or anatomical abnormality, and the severity of illness (<img> table 5). (See "<u>Pneumonia in children: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and etiology</u>", section on 'Etiologic agents'.)

**Physical examination** â€” Important aspects of the examination include the following (<img> table 6):

- **General appearance** â€“ In the young infant, assessment of general appearance includes the ability to attend to the environment, to feed, to vocalize, and to be consoled. State of awareness and cyanosis should be assessed in all children, although children may be hypoxemic without cyanosis. Most children with radiographically confirmed pneumonia appear ill [19]. Infants younger than three months of age who are toxic appearing require a

full evaluation for sepsis and other serious bacterial infections. (See "<u>The febrile infant (29 to 90 days of age): Outpatient evaluation</u>", section on 'Ill-appearing infants'.)

- **Fever** â€“ Fever is a common manifestation of pneumonia in children [10]. However, it is nonspecific and variably present. Infants younger than three months of age who are febrile may require a full evaluation for sepsis and other serious bacterial infections. (See <u>The febrile infant (29 to 90 days of age): Outpatient evaluation</u>, section on 'Evaluation'.)

Fever may be the only sign of occult pneumonia in young children with fever â‰¥39Â°C (102.2Â°F). In one report, 26 percent of 146 children (<5 years) with fever â‰¥39Â°C, no clinical evidence of pneumonia or other localizing signs, and peripheral white blood cell count â‰¥20,000/microL had radiographic evidence of pneumonia [7].

Young infants ages two weeks to four months may have afebrile pneumonia caused by *C. trachomatis* or other pathogens. These children often have milder symptoms than CAP caused by other bacteria. (See "<u>Chlamydia trachomatis infections in newborns and young infants</u>", section on 'Pneumonia'.)

- **Respiratory distress** â€“ Signs of respiratory distress include tachypnea, hypoxemia (peripheral arterial oxygen saturation [SpO<sub>2</sub>] <90 percent on room air), increased work of breathing (intercostal, subcostal, or suprasternal retractions; nasal flaring; grunting; use of accessory muscles), apnea, and altered mental status [1]. Hypoxemia is a sign of severe disease and an indication for hospital admission [<u>1,2</u>]. The presence of grunting has been associated with severe disease and impending respiratory failure [20].

Overall, signs of respiratory distress are more specific than fever or cough for a diagnosis of pneumonia but less sensitive [4]. Children with pneumonia often have tachypnea, but tachypnea is less predictive of radiographically confirmed pneumonia than other signs of respiratory distress, especially early in the course of illness (eg, less than three days) [<u>4,21</u>]. On the other hand, lack of tachypnea may be helpful in excluding pneumonia. In a systematic review of studies evaluating the probability of radiographically confirmed pneumonia in children based on clinical examination findings, the probability of pneumonia was lower if the respiratory rate was â‰¤40 breaths per minute (likelihood ratio [LR] 0.41, 95% CI 0.17-0.99) [4].

Signs of respiratory distress that are more predictive of pneumonia include retractions, head bobbing, nasal flaring, and hypoxemia (defined differently in different studies, usually SpO<sub>2</sub> <94 to 96 percent in room air) [<u>4,19,22,23</u>]. However, the absence of these findings does not exclude pneumonia. In a systematic review of studies evaluating the probability of radiographically confirmed pneumonia based on clinical examination findings, the probability of pneumonia was higher if signs of increased work of breathing (eg, retractions, nasal flaring, grunting) were present (LRs 1.9-2.7, 95% CI 1.2-5.1) [4]. The absence of these findings had minimal impact on the probability of pneumonia, which was not statistically significant.

- **Lung examination** â€“ Auscultation of all lung fields should be performed in children with suspected pneumonia. However, with the exception of wheezing, auscultatory findings have less interobserver agreement than visible findings, such as retractions or increased respiratory rate [<u>24</u>].

Examination findings consistent with radiographically confirmed pneumonia include [<u>25,26</u>]:

- Crackles
- Signs of consolidated lung parenchyma
  - Decreased breath sounds
  - Bronchial breath sounds (louder than normal and higher-pitched during expiration, with short inspiratory and long expiratory phases)
  - Egophony (E to A change)
  - Bronchophony (the distinct transmission of sounds such as the syllables of "ninety-nine")
  - Whispered pectoriloquy (transmission of whispered syllables)
  - Increased tactile fremitus (increased vibration when the patient says "ninety-nine")
  - Dullness to percussion

- Wheezing â€“ Wheezing is more common in pneumonia caused by atypical bacteria and viruses [<u>12,27</u>] than typical bacteria (see 'Bacterial versus viral etiology' above); also a sign of bronchiolitis or asthma

- Signs of pleural effusion â€“ Findings suggestive of pleural effusion include chest pain with splinting, dullness to percussion, distant breath sounds, and pleural friction rub (see "Epidemiology, clinical presentation, and evaluation of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children", section on 'Clinical presentation')

**Radiographs** â€” Children with mild pneumonia who are well enough to be treated as outpatients do not require chest radiographs to confirm the diagnosis [<u>28,29</u>]. However, if a child has a history of a previous pneumonia episode, the child should have chest radiographs obtained to evaluate for a missed foreign body or anatomic abnormality (ie, risk factors for recurrent pneumonia).

**Establishing the diagnosis** â€” The diagnosis of pneumonia is established in a child who has fever and cough, evidence by history or on physical examination of an infectious pulmonary process (ðŸ“‹ <u>table 3</u> and ðŸ“‹ <u>table 6</u>), and symptoms or signs of respiratory distress. Tachypnea, nasal flaring, grunting, retractions, and hypoxia increase the likelihood of pneumonia [<u>4</u>]. The absence of tachypnea may be helpful in excluding pneumonia; however, the absence of other

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/community-acquired-pneumonia-in-children-clinical-features-and-diagnosis/print?search=pneumonia&source... 6/52

3/18/26, 5:09 PM Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis - UpToDate

respiratory signs does not [4]. Many children with a viral upper respiratory tract infection have cough and fever; however, they do not have signs of respiratory distress. Although no single symptom or sign is pathognomonic for pneumonia in children, the longer that fever, cough, and respiratory findings are present, the greater the likelihood of pneumonia [4,5]. Neither a radiologic nor microbiologic evaluation is necessary to confirm the diagnosis of mild CAP in children (<u>table 5</u>) [30].

In resource-limited countries where there is a high prevalence of pneumonia, a single positive respiratory sign increases the certainty of pneumonia [6]. The World Health Organization uses tachypnea (>60 breaths per minute in infants <2 months; >50 breaths per minute in infants 2 to 12 months; >40 breaths per minute in children 1 to 5 years; and >20 breaths per minute in children â‰¥5 years) as the sole criterion to define pneumonia in children with cough or difficulty breathing [31]. In one study conducted in rural Uganda, the addition of a semiquantitative point-of-care C-reactive protein (CRP) test result >40 mg/L was used as a criterion for the prescription of an antibiotic [32]. During the preintervention period, 92 percent of children with tachypnea received an antibiotic prescription compared with 71 percent during the intervention period, with no increase in adverse outcomes.

In resource-abundant countries with a lower prevalence of pneumonia, the presence of multiple respiratory signs (eg, hypoxia, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions) in addition to tachypnea is used to increase the certainty of pneumonia [4,33].

## **Assessing severity** â€” An assessment of pneumonia severity is necessary to determine the appropriate setting of care. The severity of pneumonia is generally assessed by the child's degree of respiratory distress and overall clinical appearance and behavior, including an assessment of their degree of awareness and willingness to eat or drink (<u>table 5</u>) [1,2].

<u>Severity of community-acquired pneumonia in infants and children</u>

Table 5 - larger image below

Signs and symptoms that are consistent with mild pneumonia include mild or no tachypnea, normal SpO<sub>2</sub> (â‰¥90 percent on room air), and normal mental status. Signs and symptoms of severe pneumonia include severe tachypnea, SpO<sub>2</sub> <90 percent, grunting, and altered mental status.

A systematic review of studies predicting pneumonia severity in children suggests that hypoxemia, altered mental status, age <3 to 6 months, dyspnea, multilobar infiltrates, and moderate or large pleural effusions are the factors most predictive of severe pneumonia [34]. Nevertheless, standardized criteria for mild and severe pneumonia in children are lacking.

- **Comorbid asthma and viral respiratory infection** â€“ Young children with asthma who have viral respiratory infections can be misdiagnosed as having community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) [35]. Many such children have respiratory distress and may have hypoxemia. The diagnosis of CAP and treatment with antibiotics must be carefully considered in young children who have a prodrome compatible with a viral respiratory infection and are wheezing, even if there are pulmonary infiltrates (versus atelectasis) on chest radiograph. (See <u>"Asthma in children younger than 12 years: Initial evaluation and diagnosis</u>", section on '<u>Respiratory tract infections</u>'.))

# DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

- **Upper respiratory tract infection with cough** â€“ Many children with a viral upper respiratory tract infection have cough and fever; however, they do not have signs of respiratory distress. (See "<u>The common cold in children: Clinical features and diagnosis</u>", section on '<u>Symptoms and signs</u>'.))

- **Bronchiolitis** â€“ Infants and young children with bronchiolitis typically have cough and fever. The fever with bronchiolitis is usually â‰¤38.3Â°C (101Â°F), which occurs early in the disease presentation. Wheezing is a prominent component of illness. Bronchiolitis is most common during the first year of life and rarely affects children who are older than two years. (See <u>"Bronchiolitis in infants and children: Clinical features and diagnosis</u>", section on '<u>Clinical features</u>'.))

- **Asthma** â€“ Most children with pneumonia do not wheeze, although wheezing can accompany atypical pneumonia. Children whose cough and wheezing are caused by asthma do not have a fever. (See <u>"Asthma in children younger than 12 years: Initial evaluation and diagnosis</u>", section on '<u>Symptoms</u>'.))

- **Foreign body aspiration** â€“ Foreign body aspiration must be considered in young children with a cough. The aspiration event may not have been witnessed. (See <u>"Airway foreign bodies in children</u>", section on '<u>Presentation</u>'.))

- **Other causes of tachypnea in infants and young children** â€“ Other causes of tachypnea, with or without fever and cough, in infants and young children include [36]:
  - Heart failure (see <u>"Heart failure in children: Etiology, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis</u>", section on '<u>Clinical manifestations</u>')
  - Sepsis (see <u>"Sepsis in children: Definitions, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis</u>" and <u>"Neonatal bacterial sepsis: Clinical features and diagnosis in neonates â‰¥35 weeks of gestation"</u>)
  - Metabolic acidosis (see <u>"Approach to the child with metabolic acidosis</u>", section on '<u>Acute metabolic acidosis</u>')

- **Vaping-associated pulmonary illness** â€“ In adolescents and young adults, use of electronic cigarette devices to inhale aerosolized substances (ie, "vaping") has been associated with a severe pulmonary illness that shares symptoms with pneumonia (eg, shortness of breath, fever, chest pain) [37,38]. Vaping-associated pulmonary illness is discussed separately. (See <u>"Vaping and e-cigarettes"</u>, section on 'Aerosol (also known as vapor) exposure'.)

- **Noninfectious mimics of pneumonia** â€“ Noninfectious mimics of pneumonia can usually be distinguished from infectious pneumonia by history and/or associated clinical features. In some cases, laboratory studies or imaging may be necessary. The table presents a list of noninfectious conditions (<u>table 7</u>).

- **Other considerations**

- **Lemierre syndrome** â€“ Lemierre syndrome (septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein) is an important consideration in adolescents and young adults whose illness began with pharyngitis. In Lemierre syndrome, the vessels of the carotid sheath become infected (typically with *Fusobacterium* spp), leading to bacteremia and metastatic spread of infection to the lungs and mediastinum. (See <u>"Lemierre syndrome: Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein"</u>.)

- **Comorbid noninfectious lung disease** â€“ Rare, noninfectious lung diseases may present with an intercurrent infectious illness. These conditions should be considered, especially if the acute illness is atypical or the radiographic and clinical findings do not resolve as expected with uncomplicated CAP.

Causes of noninfectious lung disease include:
  - Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (see <u>"Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis in children"</u>)
  - Eosinophilic pneumonia (see <u>"Idiopathic acute eosinophilic pneumonia"</u>)
  - Acute interstitial pneumonitis (see <u>"Acute interstitial pneumonia (Hamman-Rich syndrome)"</u>)
  - Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (see <u>"Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia"</u>)

## COMPLICATIONS

Bacterial pneumonias are more likely than atypical bacterial or viral pneumonias to be associated with complications involving the respiratory tract.

- **Parapneumonic pleural effusion and empyema** â€“ A child who presents with pneumonia may already have signs and symptoms of an effusion or empyema, or these may develop over the few days following initiation of treatment [39]. Hypoalbuminemia is common in children with parapneumonic effusions, and hypogammaglobulinemia may be encountered. The clinical features and evaluation of parapneumonic effusion (<u>image 2A-B</u>) and empyema in children are discussed separately. (See <u>"Epidemiology, clinical presentation, and evaluation of</u>

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/community-acquired-pneumonia-in-children-clinical-features-and-diagnosis/print?search=pneumonia&source... 9/52

3/18/26, 5:09 PM Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis - UpToDate
- **Necrotizing pneumonia** â€“ Necrotizing pneumonia, a serious complication of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), should be considered in a child with prolonged fever or septic appearance [40]. Clinical manifestations of necrotizing pneumonia are similar to those of uncomplicated pneumonia, but they are more severe [41-43]. Necrotizing pneumonia usually follows pneumonia caused by particularly virulent bacteria [40] and is generally accompanied by parapneumonic effusion/empyema. *Streptococcus pneumoniae* (especially serotype 3 and serogroup 19) is the most common cause of necrotizing pneumonia (image 3) [44-47]. S. aureus and group A Streptococcus may also cause necrotizing pneumonia, and necrotizing pneumonia due to *M. pneumoniae*, Legionella, and Aspergillus has been reported [43,46,48-51].

parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children" and "Management and prognosis of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children".)

If the diagnosis remains uncertain, necrotizing pneumonia can be confirmed by Doppler ultrasonography, chest radiograph (which demonstrates a radiolucent lesion) (image 1), or contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) (image 3) [52,53]. The findings on chest radiograph may lag behind those of CT, and Doppler ultrasonography may detect necrotic changes earlier than CT [50,54].

- **Lung abscess** â€“ Lung abscess should be suspected when consolidation is unusually persistent, when pneumonia remains persistently round or masslike, or when the volume of the involved lobe is increased (as suggested by a bulging fissure) [55,56]. Clinical manifestations of lung abscess are nonspecific and similar to those of pneumonia [55], and the course may be indolent. Manifestations include fever, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, anorexia, hemoptysis, and putrid breath [40,57-59], and they are often accompanied by a parapneumonic effusion [39,60,61]. The average duration of fever is four to eight days.

A lung abscess is composed of an accumulation of inflammatory cells accompanied by tissue destruction or necrosis that produces one or more cavities in the lung [55]. Abscess formation may result from inadequate or delayed treatment of lobar pneumonia or, more commonly, develops one to two weeks following an aspiration event. Other predisposing factors include airway obstruction and a congenitally abnormal lung [55]. Anaerobic flora of the upper respiratory tract and S. aureus are the organisms most frequently involved [36].

The diagnosis of lung abscess is suggested by a chest radiograph demonstrating a thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level (image 1) [55]. Contrast-enhanced CT confirms the diagnosis in questionable clinical situations or if confirmation of the diagnosis is necessary before invasive interventions are performed (eg, percutaneous aspiration, placement of a drainage catheter) [52]. Interventional radiology may be helpful in obtaining a specimen from the abscess cavity for diagnostic studies.

Eighty to 90 percent of lung abscesses in children resolve with antibiotic therapy alone and spontaneous drainage through the tracheobronchial tree, provided that any bronchial obstruction has resolved or, in the case of a foreign body, been removed [57].

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/community-acquired-pneumonia-in-children-clinical-features-and-diagnosis/print?search=pneumonia&sour... 10/52

3/18/26, 5:09 PM Community-<u>acquired pneumonia in children</u>: Clinical features and diagnosis - UpToDate

- **Pneumatocele** â€“ Pneumatoceles are thin-walled, air-containing cysts of the lung, which are most often discovered incidentally on imaging performed for evaluation of pneumonia or its complications. They are classically associated with *S. aureus* but may occur with a variety of organisms [62,63]. Pneumatoceles frequently occur in association with empyema [62]. Most pneumatoceles involute spontaneously [62,64,65]. However, on occasion, pneumatoceles may result in pneumothorax [63].

- **Hyponatremia** â€“ Hyponatremia (serum sodium concentration â‰¤135 mEq/L) occurs in approximately 45 percent of children with CAP and one-third of children hospitalized with CAP, but is usually mild (ie, serum sodium concentration >130 and â‰¤135 mEq/L) [66-70]. Hyponatremia is associated with increased length of hospital stay, additional complications, and mortality and may be associated with inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone [66,67,69,70]. (See "Pathophysiology and etiology of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD)", section on 'Pulmonary disease'.)

## SETTING OF CARE

Most patients with mild pneumonia can be treated in the outpatient setting. Indications for hospitalization include moderate to severe respiratory distress, hypoxemia (peripheral arterial oxygen saturation [SpO<sub>2</sub>] <90 percent on room air), toxic appearance, and inability of the caregiver to care for the child at home. Most children less than six months of age also require hospitalization. Details about these and additional indications for hospitalization are discussed separately (<u>table 8</u>). (See "Pneumonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment", section on 'Indications for hospitalization'.)

## ADDITIONAL DIAGNOSTIC TESTING

**Indications for additional diagnostic testing** â€” Chest imaging is indicated for children admitted to the hospital to confirm the diagnosis, assess for complications, and document the size and character of parenchymal infiltrates. It is also indicated for children with a history of a previous pneumonia episodes to evaluate for a missed foreign body or anatomic abnormality (ie, risk factors for recurrent pneumonia).

A microbiologic evaluation to definitively determine the etiology of the pneumonia is indicated for children admitted to the hospital. Although the etiologic agent may be suggested by clinical presentation, epidemiologic considerations, and chest radiographic patterns, neither clinical nor

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/community-acquired-pneumonia-in-children-clinical-features-and-diagnosis/print?search=pneumonia&sour... 11/52

radiologic features reliably distinguish between typical bacterial, atypical bacterial, and viral pneumonia. (See <u>'Bacterial versus viral etiology'</u> above and <u>"Pneumonia in children: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and etiology"</u>, section on '<u>Etiologic agents</u>'.))

Testing for critical microbes is indicated if there is a local outbreak. (See <u>'Critical microbes'</u> below.)

**Chest imaging** â€” Chest imaging typically consists of radiographs. Bedside lung ultrasonography has been used to detect lung consolidation in pediatric emergency and inpatient settings [71-75]. However, diagnostic accuracy appears to be affected by the level of experience of the sonographer [76].

- **Views** â€“ Radiographic views depend upon the age of the child [77]. In children older than four years, the frontal posteroanterior (PA) upright chest view is usually obtained to minimize the size of the cardiac shadow [78]. In younger children, the anteroposterior (AP) supine view is preferred because the child's position does not affect the size of the cardiothoracic shadow in this age group and immobilization is easier, improving the likelihood of an adequate inspiration [78].

There is a lack of consensus regarding the need for lateral views to demonstrate infiltrates that may be obscured by the dome of the diaphragm or the cardiac shadow on AP or PA views [<u>1,2,55,79</u>]. In a review of chest radiographs in 201 children with pneumonia, the lateral film was abnormal in 91 percent of 109 children with definite pneumonia [80]. However, the AP or PA views also demonstrated pneumonia in all but three cases. A lateral view may be more valuable in settings where the radiographs are interpreted by nonradiologists.

Of note, the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society and Infectious Diseases Society of America suggest PA and lateral views for all children who are hospitalized for management of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) [1].

A lateral decubitus view (with the affected side down) may be needed to identify a pleural effusion. (See <u>"Epidemiology, clinical presentation, and evaluation of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children"</u>, section on '<u>Radiologic evaluation</u>'.))

- **Findings** â€“ Radiographic features do not reliably differentiate between typical bacterial, atypical bacterial, and viral pneumonia [8,81-83] and should be used in conjunction with clinical findings to make therapeutic decisions (ðŸ“Š table 2) [<u>2,84-87</u>].

In children with viral pneumonia, interstitial infiltrates are the primary radiographic finding.

Radiographic features that are more often associated with a bacterial etiology include:

- Segmental and lobar consolidation â€“ Segmental and lobar consolidation are reasonably specific for bacterial pneumonia but lack sensitivity [86,88-90]. These findings are the most common ones associated with *M. pneumoniae* (37 percent) [91]. Radiologic features of

segmental consolidation are not always easy to distinguish from segmental collapse (atelectasis), which is seen in approximately 25 percent of children with bronchiolitis [<u>92,93</u>].

- Pulmonary consolidation â€“ Pulmonary consolidation in young children sometimes appears to be spherical (ie, "round pneumonia") (<u>image 4</u>) [<u>94,95</u>]. Round pneumonias tend to be >3 cm, solitary, and posteriorly located [<u>95,96</u>]. *S. pneumoniae* is the most common bacterial etiology of round pneumonia; additional bacterial causes include other streptococci, *H. influenzae*, *S. aureus*, and *M. pneumoniae* [<u>86,97</u>].

- Peribronchial infiltrates â€“ Peribronchial infiltrates are suggestive of *M. pneumoniae* pneumonia (27 percent) (<u>image 5</u>) [<u>91</u>]. However, *S. pneumoniae* has occasionally been associated with peribronchial infiltrates in children.

- Hyperinflation with interstitial infiltrates â€“ Hyperinflation with interstitial infiltrates is characteristic of afebrile pneumonia of infancy typically caused by *C. trachomatis*. (See "<u>Chlamydia trachomatis infections in newborns and young infants</u>", section on 'Pneumonia'.)

- Pneumatoceles, cavitations, large pleural effusions, and necrotizing processes â€“ Complications of pneumonia (eg, pneumatoceles, cavitations, large pleural effusions (<u>image 2A</u> and <u>image 2B</u>), necrotizing processes (<u>image 3</u>) suggest a typical bacterial etiology (eg, *S. pneumoniae*, *S. aureus*, *Streptococcus pyogenes*) and, rarely, *M. pneumoniae*. Mediastinal and/or hilar adenopathy suggests a mycobacterial (eg, tuberculosis) or fungal (eg, histoplasmosis) etiology, although hilar adenopathy can also be seen in pneumococcal pneumonia.

- Although a negative chest radiograph excludes pneumonia in most children â‰¥3 months of age [<u>98,99</u>], radiographic findings may lag behind clinical findings [<u>100</u>], and patients who are hypovolemic may have normal-appearing chest radiographs before volume repletion.

## **Microbiologic testing** â€” Our approach to microbiologic testing is generally consistent with that of the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society and the Infectious Diseases Society of America clinical practice guidelines [<u>1</u>]. (See '<u>Society guideline links</u>' below.)

## **Blood cultures** â€” We obtain blood cultures in children who require hospitalization because they are more likely to have bacteremia than those who are treated in the outpatient setting. (See "<u>Detection of bacteremia: Blood cultures and other diagnostic tests</u>".)

Observational studies conducted in the postpneumococcal conjugate vaccine era demonstrate prevalences of bacteremic pneumonia ranging from 2.2 to 7 percent in hospitalized children who had blood cultures obtained [<u>104-106</u>]. In a prospective study, blood cultures were obtained in 91 percent of 2358 children who were hospitalized with radiographically confirmed pneumonia and were positive in 2.2 percent (95% CI 1.6-2.9 percent) [<u>106</u>]. Most isolates were susceptible to penicillin. *S. pneumoniae* (46 percent), *S. aureus* (6 percent), and *S. pyogenes* (9 percent) were the most frequently isolated pathogens. In this and other observational studies, the prevalence of bacteremia was increased in patients with complicated pneumonia or pneumonia-related metastatic complications (eg, osteomyelitis) [<u>104-110</u>].

Targeting blood cultures to children who are at increased risk for bacteremia (eg, those with pleural effusion/empyema, admission to the intensive care unit, or immunosuppression) may be clinically effective and reduce costs [<u>110,111</u>]. However, determining which children are at risk for bacteremia at the time of admission can be difficult. In one multicenter study, 6 of the 26 patients with bacteremia were initially thought to have uncomplicated pneumonia [<u>104</u>].

## **Sputum Gram stain and culture** â€” We obtain sputum samples for Gram stain and culture in children who require hospital admission if they are able to produce sputum [<u>1</u>]. Children younger than five years usually swallow sputum, so it is rarely available for examination.

Although good-quality sputum samples can be obtained by sputum induction [<u>112,113</u>], sputum induction is unpleasant. In addition, in a prospective study of the etiology of pneumonia in hospitalized children <18 years of age, bacterial pathogens were isolated from most induced sputum cultures regardless of sputum quality or whether the child had radiographically confirmed pneumonia, suggesting identification of oropharyngeal carriage rather than the pathogenic etiology of the pneumonia [<u>113</u>].

An aggressive approach to determining a definitive microbial diagnosis is necessary for immunocompromised patients with pneumonia that requires hospitalization. Invasive procedures may be required to obtain a satisfactory specimen. For patients with an

However, the protected specimen brush technique has been utilized in some settings. Quantitative bacterial cultures may differentiate colonization from true lower respiratory tract infection.
