# GRAPHICS

## Table 1: Pneumonia terminology

| Term                                               | Definition                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Classification by site of acquisition**          |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)                 | An acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma acquired outside of health care settings                                                                                                                                                     |
| Nosocomial pneumonia                               | An acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma acquired in hospital settings, which encompasses hospital-acquired pneumonia and ventilator-associated pneumonia                                                                             |
| Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP)                  | Pneumonia acquired â‰¥48 hours after hospital admission; includes both HAP and VAP                                                                                                                                                            |
| Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)              | Pneumonia acquired â‰¥48 hours after endotracheal intubation                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Non-ventilated hospital-acquired pneumonia (nvHAP) | Pneumonia that develops in hospitalized patients who are not on mechanical ventilation nor underwent extubation within 48 hours before pneumonia developed                                                                                  |
| Health care-associated pneumonia (HCAP)            | Retired term, which referred to pneumonia acquired in health care facilities (eg, nursing homes, hemodialysis centers) or after recent hospitalization\*                                                                                    |
| **Classification by etiology**                     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Atypical pneumonia                                 | Pneumonia caused by "atypical"â€¡ pathogens including *Legionella* spp, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia psittaci*, *Coxiella burnetii*                                                                            |
| Aspiration pneumonia                               | Pneumonia resulting from entry of gastric or oropharyngeal fluid, which may contain bacteria and/or exogenous substances (eg, ingested food particles or liquids, mineral oil, salt or fresh water) or be of low pH, into the lower airways |
| Chemical pneumonitis                               | Aspiration of substances (eg, acidic gastric fluid) that cause an inflammatory reaction in the lower airways, independent of bacterial infection                                                                                            |
| Bacterial aspiration pneumonia                     | An active infection caused by inoculation of large amounts of bacteria into the lungs via orogastric contents                                                                                                                               |

* The term HCAP was used to identify patients at risk for infection with multidrug-resistant pathogens. This categorization may have been overly sensitive, leading to increased, inappropriately broad antibiotic use.

â€¡ The origin of the term "atypical" is a matter of debate. The term may refer to the fact that these organisms are not "typical" bacteria (eg, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*), which can be identified by standard microbiologic techniques. Others suggest that atypical refers to the mild nature of the pneumonia caused by some of these organisms compared with pneumonia caused by *S. pneumoniae*.

CAP: community-acquired pneumonia; CURB-65: confusion, uremia, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age â‰¥65 years; ED: emergency department; FiO<sub>2</sub>: fraction of inspired oxygen; ICU: intensive care unit; PaO<sub>2</sub>: partial pressure of oxygen; PSI: Pneumonia Severity Index.

* Among the available scoring systems for determining the need for admission in patients with CAP, we prefer the PSI because it is the best studied and validated. If a less complex scoring system is desired, the CURB-65 score is a reasonable alternative, although its effectiveness and safety in guiding the initial site of treatment have not been empirically assessed. Refer to the UpToDate topic on assessing severity and determining the appropriate site of care in patients with CAP for additional details and to access PSI and CURB-65 calculators.

â€  Scoring systems, such as the PSI and CURB-65, and clinical criteria are intended to supplement rather than override the judgment of the physician. Factors other than the predictors included in the rules and the clinical criteria may be important when making an admission decision or selecting the site of inpatient care. As examples, patients with early signs of sepsis or rapidly progressive illness are not well represented by severity scores. Patients with these features may warrant hospitalization and/or ICU admission regardless of score. Conversely, older age may be overrepresented in severity scores; this should be taken into account when determining site of care.

<sup>Î”</sup> Using the CURB-65 score, if the patient has a score of 1 because he or she is â‰¥65 years of age and he or she has no major comorbidities, hospital admission is not necessarily indicated.

<sup>â—‡</sup> Although a definitive etiologic diagnosis is often not established until after the site of treatment decision has been made, clinical or epidemiologic evidence favoring pathogens associated with rapidly progressive forms of pneumonia (eg, postinfluenza bacterial pneumonias, severe acute respiratory syndrome, Middle East respiratory syndrome, avian influenza [eg, H5N1, H7N9], *Legionella* pneumonia, coronavirus disease 2019) indicate a need to perform close clinical follow-up to monitor severity of illness particularly for patients initially deemed low risk at presentation and treated outside of the hospital setting.

<sup>Â§</sup> Some PSI class II and III patients may benefit from in-home health care support, also termed "hospital-at-home" (eg, a visiting nurse, intravenous fluids, intravenous antibiotics).

# Table 5: Community-acquired pneumonia: Initial evaluation and site of care based on severity assessment in adults

|              | Severity score\*                                                                                                   | Site of care         | Microbiologic evaluation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Mild**     | PSI: I or II<br/>\*\*or\*\*<br/>CURB-65: 0â€¡                                                                        | Ambulatory care      | - COVID-19 and influenza testing when incidence is high and results would change managementÎ”<br/>- Otherwise, testing is usually not needed                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Moderate** | PSI: III or IV<br/>\*\*or\*\*<br/>CURB-65: 1â€¡ to 2                                                                 | General medical ward | - Blood cultures<br/>- Sputum Gram stain and culture<br/>- Urine streptococcal antigen<br/>- \*Legionella\* testingâ—‡<br/>- Testing for respiratory viruses during respiratory virus season or when community incidence is high (PCR preferred)Â§<br/>- HIV screeningÂ¥                                                             |
| **Severe**   | PSI: IV or V<br/>\*\*or\*\*<br/>CURB-65: â‰¥3<br/>**and/or**<br/>Fulfillment of ATS/IDSA criteria for ICU admissionâ€  | ICU                  | - Blood cultures<br/>- Sputum Gram stain and culture<br/>- Urine streptococcal antigen test<br/>- \*Legionella\* testingâ—‡<br/>- Testing for respiratory viruses (PCR preferred)Â§<br/>- Bronchoscopy specimens for Gram stain, fungal stain, aerobic, fungal culture, and molecular testing (when feasible)â€ <br/>- HIV screeningÂ¥ |

CAP presents along a continuum of severity. For practical purposes, we typically categorize CAP as mild, moderate, or severe. Severity assessment is based on clinical judgement and can be aided by severity scores, such as the PSI or the CURB-65 score. We generally prefer the PSI as it is better validated; however, many clinicians prefer the CURB-65 as it is easier to use. The three levels of severity correspond to the three levels of care (ambulatory care, hospital admission to the general medical ward, and ICU). The severity assessment and site of care each inform the initial microbiologic evaluation and empiric antibiotic selection. For all patients, we modify our approach based on patient-specific factors such as epidemiologic exposures and ability to care for oneself at home. Refer to the UpToDate topic on the treatment of CAP for further detail.

ATS: American Thoracic Society; CAP: community-acquired pneumonia; COVID-19: coronavirus disease 2019; ICU: intensive care unit; IDSA: Infectious Diseases Society of America; PaO<sub>2</sub>/FiO<sub>2</sub>: arterial oxygen tension to fraction of inspired oxygen; PCR: polymerase chain reaction; PSI: Pneumonia Severity Index.

* Severity scores should be used as an adjunct to clinical judgment. Patients with early signs of sepsis (eg, patients fulfilling minor ATS/IDSA criteria) or rapidly progressive illness are not well represented in severity scoring systems. Patients with these features may warrant hospitalization and/or ICU admission regardless of score. Conversely, older age may be overrepresented in severity scores; this should be taken into account when determining site of care.

<sup>â€¡</sup> Because age >65 years is a criterion in the CURB-65 score, patients with CURB-65 scores of 1 who are older than 65 years may also be reasonably treated in the ambulatory setting.

<sup>Î”</sup> Refer to the UpToDate content on the diagnosis of influenza and COVID-19 for details.

<sup>â—‡</sup> PCR on sputum sample is preferred for the diagnosis of *Legionella* spp because it detects most clinically relevant *Legionella* spp. The urine antigen test is an acceptable alternative when PCR is not available but is specific for *Legionella pneumophila* serogroup 1.

<sup>Â§</sup> The approach to testing for respiratory viruses varies among institutions. At a minimum, testing for SARS CoV-2 and influenza should be performed (PCR preferred). However, testing is often expanded to include adenovirus, parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and human metapneumovirus. The specific assay used (eg, PCR, antigen test) may also vary among institutions and multiplex PCR assays are becoming increasingly available. While use of these assays increases the likelihood of detecting a micro-organism, the predictive value of these results is not clear. For example, the detection of a viral pathogen does not rule out the possibility of bacterial coinfection. Similarly, some viral and bacterial pathogens can colonize the airways; their detection does not definitively indicate infection.

<sup>Â¥</sup> Refer to UpToDate content on screening and diagnosis of HIV infection for detail.

<sup>â€ </sup> ATS and IDSA major criteria for ICU admission include either septic shock with need for vasopressor support and/or respiratory failure with need for mechanical ventilation. If major criteria are not met, patients should also be considered for ICU admission if 3 or more of the following minor criteria are present: altered mental status, hypotension requiring fluid support, temperature <36Â°C/96.8Â°F, respiratory rate â‰¥30 breaths/minute, PaO<sub>2</sub>/FiO<sub>2</sub> ratio â‰¤250, blood urea nitrogen â‰¥20 mg/dL (7 mmol/L), leukocyte count <4000 cells/microL, platelet count <100,000/mL, or multilobar infiltrates.

<sup>â€ </sup> We generally weigh the benefits of obtaining a microbiologic diagnosis against the risks of the bronchoscopy (eg, need for intubation, bleeding, bronchospasm, pneumothorax) on a case-by-case basis. When pursuing bronchoscopy, we usually send specimens for aerobic and anaerobic culture, *Legionella* culture, fungal stain and culture, and testing for viral pathogens (influenza, adenovirus, parainfluenza, respiratory syncytial virus, and human metapneumovirus).

The most commonly identified causes of community-acquired pneumonia include respiratory viruses (particularly SARS coronavirus 2 during the pandemic), typical bacteria (eg, *S. pneumoniae*, *H. influenzae*, *M. catarrhalis*), and atypical bacteria (eg, *Legionella* spp, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *C. pneumoniae*). The relative prevalence of these pathogens varies with geography, pneumococcal vaccination rates, patient risk factors, season, and pneumonia severity. Certain epidemiologic exposures, like those listed above, also raise the likelihood of infection with a particular pathogen.

**COPD:** chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; **CA-MRSA:** community-acquired methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*; **HIV:** human immunodeficiency virus; **SARS:** severe acute respiratory syndrome.

## **Box A**

### **Risk factors**

**MRSA:**
**Strong risk factors that indicate need for empiric therapy:**
- Known colonization or prior infection with MRSA (positive rapid nasal PCR or any prior isolation)
- Gram-positive cocci in clusters on good-quality sputum Gram stain

**Other factors that raise suspicion for Pseudomonas and may indicate need for empiric therapy depending on local prevalence and overall clinical assessment:**
- Structural lung abnormalities (eg, bronchiectasis)
- Frequent COPD exacerbations requiring frequent glucocorticoid or antibiotic use

## **Box B**

- Vancomycin <sup>â€ </sup>
- Linezolid

- Gentamicin
- Tobramycin

- Ciprofloxacin

**Antipseudomonal/antipneumococcal beta-lactams:**
- Piperacillin-tazobactam <sup>â€ </sup>
- Cefepime
- Ceftazidime
- Imipenem
- Meropenem

**Antipneumococcal beta-lactams:**
- Ceftriaxone
- Cefotaxime

# Algorithm 3: **Approach to the patient with a past penicillin reaction who requires antibiotics**

```mermaid
graph TD
  N0[Based on a drug allergy history* and review of the medical record, classify past penicillin reaction as one of the following] --> N1[NOT ALLERGIC]
  N2[A] --> N3[C SERIOUS TYPES OF DELAYED REACTIONS types II, III, or IV]
  N2[A] --> N4[Past reaction was MILD, WITHOUT features of an IgE-mediated reaction]
  N2[A] --> N5[Past reaction DID HAVE IgE-mediated reaction, s]

  N8[F] --> N9[Correct or clarify the medical record]
  N10[C] --> N11[H TREATMENT OPTIONS: Aztreonam or an unrelated non-beta-lactam antibiotic NOTE: AVOID penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems. If there is a strong clinical indication for use of a penicillin, cephalosporin, or carbapenem, involve allergy and infectious diseases specialists for further management.]
  N12[D] --> N13[I TREATMENT OPTIONS: A third-, fourth-, or fifth-generation cephalosporin, a carbapenem, aztreonam, or an unrelated non-beta-lactam antibiotic OR Penicillin or first- or second-generation cephalosporin given by TEST DOSE PROCEDUREÎ”]
  N14[E] --> N15[TREATMENT OPTIONS: Third-, fourth-, or fifth a carbapenem given t OR Aztreonam or an unre NOTE: If a penicillin or a cephalosporin is strongly options, penicillin skin te]
```

This algorithm is intended for use in conjunction with the UpToDate content on choice of antibiotics in penicillin-allergic hospitalized patients. It is oriented toward hospitalized patients but also applies to outpatients if test dose procedures can be performed in an appropriately monitored setting with the staff and equipment needed to manage allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis.

IgE: immunoglobulin E.

* Ask the following:

1. What exactly were the symptoms?
   - Raised, red, itchy spots with each lesion lasting less than 24 hours (hives/urticaria)?
   - Swelling of the mouth, eyes, lips, or tongue (angioedema)?
   - Blisters or ulcers involving the lips, mouth, eyes, urethra, vagina, or peeling skin (seen in SJS, TEN, other severe type IV reactions)?
   - Respiratory or hemodynamic changes (anaphylaxis)?
   - Joint pains (seen in serum sickness)?
   - Did the reaction involve organs like the kidneys, lungs, or liver (seen in DRESS, other severe type IV reactions)?

2. What was the timing of the reaction after taking penicillin: Minutes, hours, or days later? Was it after the first dose or after multiple doses?

3. How long ago did the reaction happen? (After 10 years of avoidance, only 20% of patients with IgE-mediated penicillin allergy will still be allergic).

4. How was the reaction treated? Was there a need for urgent care or was adrenaline/epinephrine administered?

5. Has the patient tolerated similar medications, such as ampicillin, amoxicillin, or cephalexin since the penicillin reaction?

â€¡ Isolated mild hives, without other symptoms of an IgE-mediated reaction, can often occur in the setting of an infection. Patients with this history, especially if it occurred in childhood or >10 years ago, may also be considered to be at minimal risk for a recurrent serious reaction.

## Box A

### **Risk factors and other conditions that generally indicate need for empiric therapy**

**MRSA:**
- Septic shock
- Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation
- Gram-positive cocci in clusters on good-quality sputum Gram stain
- Known colonization or prior infection with MRSA (positive rapid nasal PCR or any prior isolation)
- Receipt of IV antibiotics during a hospitalization in the prior 3 months
- Recent influenza-like illness
- Necrotizing or cavitary pneumonia
- Presence of empyema
- Risk factors for MRSA colonization:
  - End-stage renal disease
  - Patients who are men who have sex with men
  - Living in crowded conditions
  - Incarceration
  - Injection drug use
  - Contact sports participation

***Pseudomonas*:</>
- Gram-negative bacilli seen on good-quality sputum Gram stain
- Known colonization or prior infection with *Pseudomonas*
- Receipt of IV antibiotics during a hospitalization in the prior 3 months
- Structural lung abnormalities (eg, bronchiectasis)
- Frequent COPD exacerbations requiring frequent glucocorticoid or antibiotic use

<sup>â™¦</sup> Regimens containing either a macrolide or fluoroquinolone have been generally comparable in clinical trials. However, many observational studies have suggested that macrolide-containing regimens are associated with better clinical outcomes for patients with severe CAP, possibly due to the immunomodulatory effects of macrolides. Furthermore, the severity of adverse effects (including the risk for *Clostridioides* [formerly *Clostridium*] difficile infection) and the risk of selection for resistance in colonizing organisms are generally thought to be greater with fluoroquinolones than with other antibiotic classes. For this reason, we generally favor a macrolide-containing regimen in this setting, unless there is a specific reason to avoid macrolides, such as patient allergy or intolerance. Recent antibiotic use should also inform the decision about the most appropriate regimen; if the patient has used a beta-lactam in the prior three months, a fluoroquinolone should be chosen if possible, and vice versa.

# Table 7: **Approach to vancomycin dosing for adults with normal kidney function**

|                                                                                                     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Loading dose** (for patients with known or suspected severe \*Staphylococcus aureus\* infection)â€  | Load 20 to 35 mg/kg (based on actual body weight, rounded to the nearest 250 mg increment; not to exceed 3000 mg). Within this range, we use a higher dose for critically ill patients; we use a lower dose for patients who are obese and/or are receiving vancomycin via continuous infusion. |
| **Initial maintenance dose and interval**                                                           | Typically 15 to 20 mg/kg every 8 to 12 hours for most patients (based on actual body weight, rounded to the nearest 250 mg increment).<br/>In general, the approach to establishing the vancomycin dose/interval is guided by a nomogram.Î”                                                      |
| ***Subsequent dose and interval adjustments***                                                      | Based on AUC-guided or trough-guided serum concentration monitoring.â—‡                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

AUC: area under the 24-hour time-concentration curve; CNS: central nervous system.

* Refer to the UpToDate topic on vancomycin dosing for management of patients with abnormal kidney function.

<sup>â€ </sup> For patients with known or suspected severe *S. aureus* infection, we suggest administration of a loading dose to reduce the likelihood of suboptimal initial vancomycin exposure. Severe *S. aureus* infections include (but are not limited to) bacteremia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint infection, pneumonia warranting hospitalization, infection involving the central nervous system, or infection causing critical illness.

<sup>Î”</sup> If possible, the nomogram should be developed and validated at the institution where it is used to best reflect the regional patient population. Refer to the UpToDate topic on vancomycin dosing for sample nomogram.

<sup>â—‡</sup> Refer to text for discussion of AUC-guided and trough-guided vancomycin dosing. For patients with severe infection, AUC-guided dosing is generally preferred if feasible<sup>[1]</sup>. For patients with CNS infection, data on optimal vancomycin dosing are limited. In such cases, most experts recommend targeting the higher end of standard drug exposure (either an AUC of 500 to 600 mgÂ·h/L or a trough concentration of 15 to 20 mcg/mL), based primarily on theoretical considerations of enhanced CNS penetration and activity; however, the benefit of this approach warrants careful consideration in patients at higher risk of nephrotoxicity. For patients with nonsevere infection who receive vancomycin for <3 days (in the setting of stable kidney function and absence of other risk factors for altered vancomycin kinetics), vancomycin concentration monitoring is often omitted; the value of such monitoring prior to achieving steady state (usually around treatment day 2 to 3) is uncertain.

# Algorithm 6: **Duration of antibiotics for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia in inpatients**

```mermaid
graph TD
  N0[A Patient with CAP who is responding to antibiotic treatment and lacks complications eg, parapneumonic effusion, empyema, lung abscess, bacteremia *] --> N1[Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia?]
  N2[B] --> N3[Yes C Treatment duration based on clinical response br â–  Minimum 7 days if early clinical response and no complications br â–  Longer courses eg, â‰¥4 weeks often needed for immunocompromised patients and those with metastatic complications]
  N2[B] --> N4[No D Do ANY of the following apply? br â–  Initial treatment not active against subsequently identified pathogen br â–  Documented Pseudomonas aeruginosa, S. aureus, Legionella spp, or an uncommon bacterial species]
  N5[D] --> N6[Yes E Individualized duration of therapy based upon the clinical response to treatment and patient comorbidities]
  N5[D] --> N7[No F Do ALL of the following apply? br â–  Afebrile for 48 to 72 hours br â–  Supplemental oxygen not needed unless required for a preexisting condition br â–  No more than one of the following: br - Heart rate 100 beats/minute br - Respiratory rate 24 breaths/minute br - Systolic blood pressure â‰¤90 mmHg]
  N8[F] --> N9[Yes G Discontinue antibiotics after 5 to 7 days]
  N8[F] --> N10[No H Continue antibiotics until clinically stable; reevaluate at 7 days]
```

For patients with CAP who have a good clinical response within the first two to three days of therapy, the duration of antibiotic treatment is generally 5 to 7 days. Longer courses may be needed for patients who are slower to improve; have CAP caused by *S. aureus*, *Pseudomonas* spp, or other less common pathogens; or when the initial antibiotic regimen was not active against a subsequently identified pathogen. Procalcitonin levels can also be used to help guide antibiotic duration. Refer to the UpToDate text for detail.

* The duration of antibiotics for patients with complications (eg, parapneumonic effusion, empyema, lung abscess, bacteremia) is longer and varies by complication; additional evaluation and/or procedures (eg, drainage of parapneumonic effusion) may be warranted.

**Differential diagnosis:**
- Other respiratory tract infections
  - Acute bronchitis
  - Upper respiratory tract infection
- Non-infectious pulmonary disorders
  - Acute exacerbations of COPD
  - Acute asthma exacerbation
  - Acute bronchiectasis exacerbation
  - Atelectasis
  - Aspiration or chemical pneumonitis
  - Drug reaction
  - EVALI
  - Interstitial lung disease
  - Lung cancer
  - Pulmonary hemorrhage
- Cardiovascular diseases
  - Heart failure with pulmonary edema
  - Pulmonary embolism
- Non-respiratory tract infections
  - Urinary tract infection
  - Intra-abdominal infection
  - Endocarditis

Once a patient with CAP is hospitalized, further management will be dictated by the patient's response to initial empiric therapy. Clinical response should be assessed daily. We generally look for:
- Subjective improvement in symptoms (cough, sputum production, dyspnea, and chest pain)
- Resolution of fever
- Normalization (ie, trend towards improvement) of heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygenation, and white blood cell count.

Most patients with CAP demonstrate some clinical improvement within 48 to 72 hours. For patients with an initial clinical diagnosis of CAP who have rapidly resolving pulmonary infiltrates, alternate diagnoses should be investigated and early discontinuation of antibiotics should be considered. Refer to UpToDate text for additional detail.

CAP: community-acquired pneumonia; COPD: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; EVALI: e-cigarette or vaping use-associated lung injury; SARS-CoV-2: severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2.

* If a microbiologic diagnosis has been made, the empiric regimen can be tailored to target the pathogen. In general, we continue intravenous antibiotic treatment until there is a clinical improvement.

Â¶ If an alternate diagnosis seems more likely, antibiotic discontinuation can be considered.

Î” Antibiotics should be broadened when worsening infection is among the suspected causes of deterioration. Antibiotic selection will vary based on patient risk factors, local epidemiology, suspected pathogens, and the initially selected regimen. Generally, regimens that include treatment for methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* and Pseudomonas, in addition to routine CAP pathogens (eg, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, Enterobacteriaceae, atypical organisms) should be selected.

â—‡ Evaluation varies based upon clinical picture but typically includes blood cultures, repeat sputum Gram stain and culture, or bronchoalveolar lavage, urine pneumococcal antigen testing, testing for Legionella, respiratory viruses including influenza and SARS-CoV-2, and chest computed tomography scan. Noninfectious causes of clinical deterioration should also be considered (eg, acute myocardial infarction, cardiac arrhythmias).

Â§ For all patients, we treat until the patient has been afebrile and clinically stable for at least 48 hours and for a minimum of five days. Patients with severe infection, chronic comorbidities, or immunocompromise may require longer courses.

Â¶ Procalcitonin can be used help guide duration of therapy in patients who are improving. Refer to UpToDate content on procalcitonin for detail.

# **Algorithm 9: Follow-up imaging for immunocompetent adults who have recovered from community-acquired pneumonia**

Follow-up imaging is not needed for most patients who have promptly recovered from CAP (eg, within 5 to 7 days for an otherwise healthy person). However, follow-up clinic visits are good opportunities to review the patient's risk for lung cancer based on age, smoking history, and recent imaging findings.

CT: computed tomography; CAP: community-acquired pneumonia.

* Criteria for lung cancer screening vary among clinical practice guidelines (eg, thresholds for age and duration of smoking therapy). Refer to UpToDate text for detail.

â€¡ Exceptions include patients who are followed radiographically for other reasons (eg, selected patients with advanced structural lung disease). Whether patients with small pleural effusions require follow-up is an open question. We generally do not obtain follow-up imaging unless the patient is slow to recover or develops new systemic or respiratory symptoms.

# Pneumonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment

**AUTHOR:** William J Barson, MD

## INTRODUCTION

Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is defined as an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma in a patient who has acquired the infection in the community, as distinguished from hospital-acquired (nosocomial) pneumonia. CAP is a common and potentially serious illness with considerable morbidity.

The inpatient treatment of CAP and hospital-acquired pneumonia in children >28 days old will be reviewed here.

Our recommendations are generally consistent with practice guidelines provided by <u>the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society/Infectious Diseases Society of America</u> and the British Thoracic Society [<u>1,2</u>]. (See 'Society guideline links' below.)

Other topics related to CAP in children and management of pneumonia in neonates are discussed separately:

- (See "<u>Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Outpatient treatment</u>".)
- (See "<u>Pneumonia in children: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and etiology</u>".)
- (See "<u>Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis</u>".)
- (See "<u>Neonatal pneumonia</u>".)

## TERMINOLOGY

This topic discusses treatment for three categories of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). These categories are defined as follows:

- **Nonsevere uncomplicated pneumonia** â€“ In this context, nonsevere pneumonia refers to pneumonia that requires hospitalization for one or more indications (eg, age, level of respiratory distress, inability of the caregiver to care for the child at home) (<u>table 1</u>). This category of treatment is only intended for children without pneumonia complications. (See '<u>Nonsevere uncomplicated pneumonia</u>' below.)

- **Severe uncomplicated pneumonia** â€“ Children with severe pneumonia are in moderate to severe distress (eg, nasal flaring, grunting, altered mental status, peripheral oxygen saturation [SpO<sub>2</sub>] <90 percent in room air, capillary refill â‰¥2 seconds) (<u>table 2</u>). This category of treatment is only intended for children without pneumonia complications. (See '<u>Severe uncomplicated pneumonia</u>' below.)

- **Complicated pneumonia** â€“ Complicated pneumonia refers to pneumonia associated with parapneumonic effusion/empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, or lung abscess. Complicated pneumonia can be associated with either nonsevere or severe clinical manifestations. Complicated pneumonia requires broader antimicrobial therapy than is used for uncomplicated pneumonia. It also may require invasive interventions to drain effusions or remove necrotic tissue. (See '<u>Complicated pneumonia</u>' below and "<u>Management and prognosis of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children</u>").

# INDICATIONS FOR HOSPITALIZATION

- **General indications for hospital admission** â€“ The decision to hospitalize a child with pneumonia is individualized based on age, underlying medical problems, and severity of illness. Indications for hospitalization include (<u>table 1</u>) [1-3]:

- Young age â€“ Hospitalization is often warranted for infants <3 to 6 months of age, unless a viral etiology or *Chlamydia trachomatis* is suspected and the infant is minimally symptomatic and not hypoxemic.
  
  - Hypoxemia (peripheral oxygen saturation [SpO<sub>2</sub>] <90 percent in room air).
  
  - Dehydration or inability to maintain hydration orally; inability to feed in an infant.

Most children who require hospitalization for pneumonia can be managed in the general inpatient pediatric unit. Indications for intensive care unit admission are outlined below.

- **Pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission** â€“ Admission to the PICU is generally warranted for children with any of the following [[1,2]]:

- Severe respiratory distress (eg, marked retractions, dyspnea, nasal flaring, grunting)

- Need for advanced respiratory support (mechanical ventilation, noninvasive ventilation [NIV])

- Moderate to severe hypoxemia (eg, requiring a high fraction of inspired oxygen [FiO<sub>2</sub>] to maintain SpO<sub>2</sub> >92 percent [eg, FiO<sub>2</sub> >0.5]))

- Recurrent episodes of apnea

- Depressed or altered mental status

- Hemodynamic instability or shock (eg, progressive tachycardia, lactic acidosis, and/or hypotension despite fluid resuscitation)

- Underlying medical condition that places the child at high risk for severe/complicated illness (eg, sickle cell disease, primary immune deficiency)

# INFECTION CONTROL MEASURES

**Rapid diagnostic tests** â€” If possible, rapid diagnostic tests should be performed at the time of admission to facilitate patient cohorting and other infection control decisions. We prefer rapid diagnostic tests to cultures because of their general availability, and their results are reported sooner. (See "Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis", section on 'Rapid diagnostic testing'.)

## General measures

- **Standard precautions** â€“ Standard precautions include hand hygiene and, if exposure to infectious material is anticipated (eg, purulent wound, respiratory secretions), the use of personal protective equipment. Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent the spread of infection. Guidelines for hand hygiene in health care settings can be accessed through the ðŸ”— Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

- **Additional infection control measures** â€“ Additional infection control measures for suspected respiratory pathogens depend on the likely pathogen. However, we favor simplifying the approach by placing all patients with suspected respiratory tract infection on both contact and droplet precautions. If measles or varicella are suspected, airborne precautions are also indicated.

Once the results of rapid diagnostic tests or cultures are available, measures can be narrowed as follows [5,6]:

- Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza, and human metapneumovirus â€“ Contact precautions (ie, gown and gloves) and mask according to standard precautions
- Influenza, rhinovirus, group A *Streptococcus* (GAS; first 24 hours of treatment), and *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* â€“ Droplet precautions (ie, mask within 3 feet)
- Adenovirus â€“ Contact and droplet precautions
- Measles â€“ Airborne precautions (ie, use of fit-tested N95 mask)
- Varicella â€“ Airborne and contact precautions
- Methicillin-susceptible *S. aureus* (MSSA) â€“ Standard precautions
- Methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA) or other multidrug-resistant organisms â€“ Contact and droplet precautions if exposed to respiratory secretions and use of dedicated patient equipment

# PRETREATMENT EVALUATION

- **Laboratory evaluation** â€“ The typical laboratory evaluation for children hospitalized with pneumonia includes a complete blood count (CBC) with differential, inflammatory markers, and serum electrolytes.

- **CBC** â€“ When assessed in conjunction with other clinical, laboratory, and radiographic features, the white blood cell (WBC) count can sometimes be helpful in distinguishing between typical bacterial, atypical bacterial, and nonbacterial causes of pneumonia:

- An elevated WBC count (>15,000/microL) is suggestive of a typical bacterial etiology [7]. However, children with *M. pneumoniae*, influenza, or adenovirus pneumonia may also have an elevated WBC count [8-10].

- A normal or reduced WBC count suggests a nonbacterial etiology. However, a severely ill patient with bacterial pneumonia may present with leukopenia with a predominance of immature cells.

- Peripheral eosinophilia is characteristic of afebrile pneumonia of infancy (typically caused by *C. trachomatis*). (See "<u>Chlamydia trachomatis infections in newborns and young infants</u>", section on 'Pneumonia'.)

- **Inflammatory markers** â€“ Baseline inflammatory markers (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR], C-reactive protein [CRP], serum procalcitonin [PCT]) obtained at admission and followed by serial measurements during treatment may provide useful information about a patient's response to therapy [1,11-16]. They may also assist with clinical management decisions (eg, when to discontinue antimicrobial therapy). (See '<u>Duration of treatment</u>' below.)

Inflammatory marker levels do not reliably differentiate between typical bacterial, atypical bacterial, and viral pneumonia, but they may be helpful for assessing the likelihood of each. In a meta-analysis of observational studies in children, an elevated CRP and PCT performed better than an elevated WBC count in distinguishing bacterial from viral pneumonia; however, the sensitivity and specificity of approximately 70 and 65 percent, respectively, are insufficiently accurate to be used in isolation [17].

In a prospective, multicenter study of 532 children hospitalized with radiographically confirmed community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), median PCT values for typical bacterial etiologies were higher than for atypical bacterial and viral etiologies, but the ranges overlapped [18]. However, no child with a serum PCT <0.1 ng/mL had a typical bacterial

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pneumonia-in-children-greater-than28-days-old-inpatient-treatment/print?search=pneumonia&source=search... 5/57

3/18/26, 5:06 PM Pneonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment - UpToDate

etiology, suggesting that this threshold may be helpful for identifying a low risk of typical bacterial CAP. CRP and PCT do not appear to be useful in predicting illness severity [<u>19</u>].

- **Serum electrolytes** â€“ We suggest measuring serum electrolytes in all children requiring hospitalization for pneumonia since dehydration and hyponatremia are common in this setting.

- **Radiographic evaluation** â€“ Children who are admitted to the hospital with pneumonia should have chest radiographs to confirm the diagnosis and assess for complications (eg, parapneumonic effusion). The radiographic evaluation is discussed in detail separately. (See <u>"Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis"</u>, section on '<u>Chest imaging</u>'.))

- **Microbiologic testing** â€“ Children who are admitted to the hospital for CAP should undergo microbiologic testing that includes rapid diagnostic testing (see <u>'Rapid diagnostic tests'</u> above), as well as blood cultures and a sputum (expectorated or induced) Gram stain and culture. The microbiologic evaluation is discussed in detail separately. (See <u>"Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis"</u>, section on '<u>Microbiologic testing</u>'.))

Microbiologic testing is necessary in all hospitalized children with CAP since the clinical, laboratory. and radiologic features do not reliably distinguish between different etiologies.
(See <u>"Pneumonia in children: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and etiology"</u>, section on '<u>Etiologic agents</u>'.))

## **SUPPORTIVE AND ADJUNCTIVE CARE**

**Antipyresis and analgesia** â€” Fever and pleuritic chest pain should be treated with antipyretics and/or analgesics (eg, <u>acetaminophen</u>, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug [NSAID]). Fever can increase tachypnea and work of breathing in infants and children with pneumonia. Pleuritic chest pain can lead to shallow breathing and impaired ability to cough. Opioid analgesia does not play any role in this setting unless the child has a chest tube in place and experiences breakthrough pain while receiving parenteral <u>ketorolac</u>.

**Respiratory support** â€” Children hospitalized with pneumonia should receive respiratory support as indicated by their clinical condition [<u>1,2</u>].

For children with hypoxemia, we suggest titrating supplemental oxygen therapy to maintain peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO<sub>2</sub>) â‰¥92 percent. Other experts use different targets for supplemental oxygen. Gentle bulb suctioning of the nares may help reduce oxygen requirements in infants and children whose nares are blocked with secretions. Minimal

handling of the child may also reduce oxygen requirements. (See "<u>Continuous oxygen delivery systems for the acute care of infants, children, and adults</u>".)

Children with severe pneumonia may require advanced respiratory support with high-flow nasal cannula, noninvasive ventilation (NIV; including continuous positive airway pressure [CPAP] and bilevel positive airway support [BPAP]), or, rarely, intubation and mechanical ventilation. Details of these modalities are beyond the scope of this topic. They are discussed separately. (See "<u>High-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy in children</u>" and "<u>Noninvasive ventilation for acute and impending respiratory failure in children</u>" and "<u>Initiating mechanical ventilation in children</u>".)

In children who are severely ill, it may be necessary to monitor carbon dioxide tension via blood gas analysis in addition to SpO<sub>2</sub> by oximetry. A capillary or venous blood sample may be used because evaluation of the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO<sub>2</sub>) does not require arterial blood. Hypercarbia is an important sign of impending respiratory failure, particularly in the young infant who is tiring but may have preserved oxygenation. Indications for carbon dioxide monitoring include signs that the child is tiring out (eg, less responsive, less active) and lack of improvement (eg, persistent severe retractions, persistent respiratory distress) after several hours of NIV.

**Fluid management** â€” Children who cannot maintain adequate fluid intake due to work of breathing, fatigue, or risk of aspiration require supplemental fluid therapy, which is usually provided with intravenous (IV) isotonic fluids [20]. Nasogastric (NG) tube hydration is usually avoided in a severely ill child because it may compromise breathing. When NG tube hydration is necessary, the smallest tube possible should be used [2]. (See "<u>Maintenance intravenous fluid therapy in children</u>".)

Children with pneumonia are at risk for syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) [21,22]. Serum electrolytes, fluid balance, and urine specific gravity should be monitored if there is clinical suspicion of SIADH [22]. Confirmation of SIADH is discussed separately. (See "<u>Pathophysiology and etiology of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD)</u>", section on 'Pulmonary disease' and "<u>Maintenance intravenous fluid therapy in children</u>".)

## Measures with unproven or no benefit

- **Antitussives** â€“ Antitussives should be avoided, as none have been found to be effective in pneumonia [23]. Symptomatic treatment of cough is discussed separately. (See "<u>The common cold in children: Management and prevention</u>", section on 'Cough'.)

- **Chest physiotherapy (CPT)** â€“ Routine use of CPT does not appear to be beneficial for children with uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) [2]. A systematic review and meta-analysis identified six trials (559 patients, ages 29 days to 12 years) assessing the

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pneumonia-in-children-greater-than28-days-old-inpatient-treatment/print?search=pneumonia&source=search... 7/57

3/18/26, 5:06 PM Pneumonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment - UpToDate

effectiveness of various CPT interventions including conventional CPT with and without positive expiratory pressure, CPAP (nasal and bubble), and assisted autogenic drainage in children hospitalized with pneumonia [24]. Of the five trials reporting changes in SpO<sub>2</sub> after the CPT intervention, two trials reported improvements in SpO<sub>2</sub> whereas three trials did not detect any improvement. There was little to no difference in length of hospital stay between children who did or did not receive CPT (based on four trials).

- **Adjunctive glucocorticoid therapy** â€“ We do not routinely provide glucocorticoid therapy to children hospitalized with pneumonia. Although some data suggest benefit, trials are limited, and more data are needed before this practice can be adopted as routine.

A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis identified three small pediatric trials assessing the effect of systemic glucocorticoid therapy in children with *M. pneumoniae* pneumonia (two trials) or CAP (one trial) [25]. There were no deaths among the 225 children enrolled in these trials. The time to clinical cure was faster for children assigned to glucocorticoid therapy compared with those in the control group (mean difference 1.6 days, 95% CI 0.6-2.6 days). Children receiving glucocorticoid therapy were also less likely to have early clinical failure (defined as radiographic progression or clinical instability at day 5 through 8) compared with those in the control group (relative risk [RR] 0.41, 95% CI 0.24-0.70). However, the clinical failure rate in the control group was unusually high (66 percent) and not consistent with contemporary practice in resource-abundant settings. Thus, this finding may not be generalizable to other settings.

In a retrospective study of 2244 children treated for CAP in the outpatient setting, 13 percent received adjunctive glucocorticoid therapy, most of whom had underlying asthma [26]. Among children without underlying asthma, use of adjunctive glucocorticoids was associated with increased likelihood of having an unplanned acute care visit for respiratory complaints within 14 days of the CAP diagnosis. This finding suggests that glucocorticoid therapy may have a detrimental effect in children with nonsevere CAP in the absence of underlying asthma.

Additional large, well-designed pediatric trials are needed to clarify the role of adjunctive glucocorticoids in treating CAP.

Table 4 - larger image below

The features often overlap, and they do not reliably distinguish between the different etiologies. Nevertheless, they can be helpful in guiding empiric therapy pending results of microbiologic testing.

We suggest that clinicians use their best judgment as to whether the child's overall clinical picture (including the presentation, laboratory results, and radiographic findings) is most consistent with typical bacterial pneumonia, atypical bacterial pneumonia, a mixed picture, or a viral illness (<u>table 4</u>).

- If the clinical picture is most consistent with typical bacterial pneumonia (eg, lobar consolidation on chest radiograph with high fever and elevated inflammatory markers), empiric therapy should target common bacterial causes of CAP (eg, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, group A *Streptococcus* [GAS], *Haemophilus influenzae*), as discussed below. (See <u>'Age-based regimens for nonsevere uncomplicated CAP'</u> below.)

- If the clinical picture is most consistent with atypical bacterial pneumonia (eg, myalgias, conjunctivitis, sore throat, rash), empiric therapy consists of a macrolide (eg, <u>azithromycin</u>) to cover atypical bacterial pathogens (*M. pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia pneumoniae*).

- If the clinical picture is mixed, combination therapy is generally appropriate (ie, an agent that covers typical bacterial pathogens plus a macrolide to cover atypical pathogens).

- If the clinical picture is most consistent with a viral infection and there is no concern for bacterial coinfection, antibiotic therapy is not necessary. Antiviral therapy should be provided if a treatable viral etiology is identified (eg, influenza or coronavirus disease 2019 [COVID-19]). For other viral pathogens (eg, respiratory syncytial virus [RSV], rhinovirus, adenovirus), treatment is supportive. (See <u>'Viral pathogens'</u> below and <u>'Confirmed viral etiology'</u> below.)

While we suggest using this approach to help guide the initial choice of empiric therapy, clinicians should recognize that making these judgments is not an exact science. Therefore, it is important to regularly reevaluate the patient to assess their response to therapy and modify treatment if necessary. (See <u>'Response to therapy'</u> below.)

Afebrile well-appearing infants between the ages of two weeks and four months may have pneumonia caused by *C. trachomatis* (sometimes called afebrile pneumonia of infancy), which is characterized by insidious onset of nasal congestion and possibly conjunctivitis, followed by gradual development of staccato cough and tachypnea. *C. trachomatis* pneumonia is typically a mild illness, and most affected infants do not require hospitalization unless their illness is associated with dehydration or other complications. *C. trachomatis* pneumonia is treated with macrolide antibiotics (eg, <u>azithromycin</u>), as discussed separately. **Infants and children 6 months to <4 years** â€” *S. pneumoniae* is the most common bacterial cause of pneumonia in this age group. A prospective population-based study of 1418 children hospitalized with radiographically confirmed CAP did not detect any differences in length of stay, intensive care admission, rehospitalization, or self-reported recovery in children who received combination therapy compared with those who received beta-lactam monotherapy [39].

## **Parenteral therapy preferred for most patients** â€” We suggest that children who require hospitalization for treatment of pneumonia be treated initially with parenteral antibiotics [<u>1</u>]. These children are typically not eating well and are receiving intravenous (IV) fluid hydration. In this setting, provide IV antibiotic therapy rather than trying to administer oral antibiotics to a sick child.

However, oral <u>amoxicillin</u> may be an acceptable alternative for infants and children who are fully immunized against Hib and *S. pneumoniae* and have nonsevere, uncomplicated pneumonia that is not thought to be due to *S. aureus* [<u>43,44</u>]. In a multicenter clinical trial in which patients with uncomplicated nonsevere CAP were randomly assigned to treatment with oral amoxicillin or IV <u>penicillin G</u>, clinical outcomes were similar in both groups [<u>45</u>]. The British Thoracic Society guidelines also suggest that oral antibiotics are safe and effective for children hospitalized with pneumonia as long as they are able to tolerate oral fluids, are not vomiting, and do not have signs of septicemia or complicated pneumonia [<u>2</u>].

## **Suspicion for specific organisms**

**S. aureus** â€” Children with pneumonia caused by *S. aureus* are typically toxic appearing with high fever and a severe, rapidly progressing illness. Staphylococcal pneumonia may be preceded by a viral respiratory tract infection (especially influenza) and may be associated with complications (eg, parapneumonic effusion/empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, lung abscess) [<u>46,47</u>]. For this reason, antistaphylococcal coverage is included in the empiric regimen for children with complicated pneumonia or severe pneumonia requiring intensive care management, as discussed below. (See '<u>Severe uncomplicated pneumonia</u>' below and '<u>Complicated pneumonia</u>' below.)

Additional guidance for selecting empiric antistaphylococcal coverage in children with suspected invasive *S. aureus* infections is summarized in the table (table 7

Testing for nasal carriage of methicillin-susceptible *S. aureus* (MSSA)/methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA) by culture or molecular tests may be helpful in reducing the use of anti-MSSA/MRSA therapy in the treatment of nonsevere uncomplicated pneumonia [<48-50>]. A negative result has a negative predictive value of approximately 95 percent for excluding MRSA pneumonia. Nevertheless, clinical judgment should be used to determine whether further testing is needed to completely rule out MRSA pneumonia.

**Viral pathogens** â€” Most children <5 years of age who are admitted to the hospital with pneumonia have viral pneumonia (eg, RSV, rhinovirus, adenovirus) [51]. This is particularly true in the absence of a lobar (or lobular) infiltrate and pleural effusion [4]. Viral pneumonia does not require empiric antibiotic therapy unless a mixed bacterial infection or secondary bacterial infection is suspected. Importantly, up to one-half of CAP in children may be of a mixed viral/bacterial etiology.

Common treatable viral causes of pneumonia include influenza and COVID-19. These are readily detectable with rapid diagnostic tests. (See '<u>Rapid diagnostic tests</u>' above and <u>'Confirmed viral etiology'</u> below.)

If a child is hospitalized during influenza season and results of rapid diagnostic testing for influenza are not readily available, empiric antiviral therapy (eg, oseltamivir) should be started pending laboratory confirmation. (See "<u>Seasonal influenza in children: Management</u>", section on '<u>Indications and preferred regimens</u>'.))

If influenza is complicated by secondary bacterial pneumonia, empiric antibiotic therapy should include coverage for *S. aureus*, including MRSA. Coinfection with influenza and *S. aureus* is particularly severe and can be rapidly fatal. (See "<u>Seasonal influenza in children: Clinical features and diagnosis</u>", section on '<u>S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, or S. aureus coinfection</u>'.))

Other considerations for antiviral therapy are discussed below. (See '<u>Confirmed viral etiology</u>' below.)

**Aspiration pneumonia** â€” For empiric treatment of aspiration pneumonia, we suggest ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin [52]. The former provides coverage for oral anaerobes as well as the usual bacterial causes of CAP (eg, *S. pneumoniae*, GAS, MSSA, *H. influenzae*). The latter's coverage is similar, except it lacks coverage against *H influenzae*, and its GAS, *S. pneumoniae*, and MSSA coverage is not as broad.

Clindamycin is preferred if MRSA is suspected and the prevalence of clindamycin resistance in the community is <15 percent [53] or if the patient has a contraindication to beta-lactam antibiotics (eg, history of IgE-mediated reaction or severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction (ðŸ“Š table 6)).

## Special situations

**Hospital-acquired pneumonia** â€” We suggest a broad-spectrum empiric antibiotic regimen for most patients with hospital-acquired pneumonia. These patients require coverage for gram-positive (eg, *S. aureus*), gram-negative (eg, Enterobacteriaceae, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*), and anaerobic pathogens (if aspiration pneumonia is a possibility). ## ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS

### Duration of treatment

- **Parenteral antibiotic duration** â€“ There are few data to guide decisions about the duration of parenteral therapy for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) [2,60]. It is common to switch from parenteral antibiotics to oral therapy once the patient is clinically improving, afebrile for 24 to 48 hours, and not vomiting [61].

- **Total antibiotic duration** â€“ The total duration of the antibiotic course is determined by the severity of the pneumonia, the causative agent, and the immune status of the host.

There are few randomized controlled trials available to guide decisions about the appropriate duration of antimicrobial therapy for radiographically confirmed childhood pneumonia that requires hospitalization [2].

- **Uncomplicated CAP** â€“ For children hospitalized with uncomplicated CAP, we generally treat with a five- to seven-day course of combined parenteral and oral therapy.

This is supported by studies demonstrating the effectiveness of shorter courses of therapy for uncomplicated pneumonia [62-64]. In a single-center observational study in children â‰¥6 months of age who were hospitalized with uncomplicated CAP, rates of treatment failure were similar among those who received antibiotic therapy for 5 to 7 days and 8 to 14 days (3 versus 6 percent; odds ratio [OR] 0.48, 95% CI 0.18-1.20) [62]. Treatment failure was defined as a composite of unanticipated emergency department or outpatient visits, readmission, or death within 30 days after completion of antibiotics.

In a subsequent trial, patients with uncomplicated CAP who were randomly assigned to receive 5 days of antibiotics had a similar response to those assigned to receive 10 days of antibiotics [64]. Additionally, fewer patients who received the shorter course of antibiotics had antibiotic resistance genes detected on end-of-treatment throat swabs.

Randomized trials in adult patients with mild to moderate CAP also suggest that outcomes in patients treated for less than seven days are similar to those in patients treated longer. These trials are discussed separately. (See "Treatment of community-acquired pneumonia in adults in the outpatient setting", section on 'Duration of therapy'.)

- **Complicated pneumonia** â€“ Treatment of complications (such as parapneumonic effusion/empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, and lung abscess) requires a prolonged

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pneumonia-in-children-greater-than28-days-old-inpatient-treatment/print?search=pneumonia&source=searc... 21/57

3/18/26, 5:06 PM
Pneumonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment - UpToDate

course of antibiotic therapy [65]. The duration is determined by the clinical response but is usually either a total of three to four weeks or another two weeks after the patient is afebrile and has improved clinically. Some infectious disease specialists use an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) value of <20 mm/hour as a laboratory indicator that the duration of therapy has been sufficient. (See 'Complicated pneumonia' above.)

The duration of treatment for lung abscess is also determined by the radiographic resolution of the abscess or stabilization of a small lesion.

**Response to therapy** â€” The following clinical parameters should be monitored to assess response to treatment [1,2]:

- Temperature
- Respiratory rate
- Heart rate
- Peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO<sub>2</sub>)
- Work of breathing (eg, retractions, nasal flaring, grunting)
- Mental status
- Ability to maintain oral intake and hydration
- Chest examination (extent of abnormal or absent breath sounds, extent of dullness to percussion)

The frequency of monitoring depends upon the severity of illness. In patients who are receiving oxygen therapy, SpO<sub>2</sub> should be evaluated regularly.

The respiratory status of children with uncomplicated CAP who are appropriately treated should improve within 48 to 72 hours [1]. However, fevers may persist for several days after initiation of appropriate therapy [52].

**Treatment failure** â€” In children with CAP who fail to improve as anticipated, the following possibilities must be considered [1,2,66,67]:

- Alternative or coincident diagnoses (eg, foreign body aspiration) (see "Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis", section on 'Differential diagnosis')
- Ineffective antibiotic coverage (lack of coverage for the actual etiology or resistant organism)

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pneumonia-in-children-greater-than28-days-old-inpatient-treatment/print?search=pneumonia&source=searc... 22/57

3/18/26, 5:06 PM Pneonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment - UpToDate

- Development of complications (see "Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis", section on 'Complications')

- Underlying immunodeficiency condition

The history should be reviewed with special attention to the possibility of foreign body aspiration and geographic or environmental exposures associated with pathogens not treated by the empiric regimen (<u>table 9</u>).

A repeat peripheral white blood cell (WBC) count and inflammatory markers should be sent because they may provide information about disease progression.

Repeat radiographs or additional imaging studies should be obtained to help assess the degree of parenchymal involvement and evaluate for complications or anatomic abnormalities [1].

If not already completed, a microbiologic evaluation should be done to help direct antibiotic therapy. (See "Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis", section on 'Microbiologic testing'.)

Invasive procedures may be necessary to obtain lower respiratory tract specimens for culture and other studies in children in whom an etiologic diagnosis is necessary and has not been established by other means. These procedures are typically reserved for seriously ill patients whose condition is worsening despite empiric therapy, individuals with significant comorbidities (eg, immune compromise), and those with complications [68-71] as follows:

- Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) â€“ For samples obtained via bronchoscopy, quantitative culture techniques are suggested to differentiate true infection from upper airway contamination [72-74].

- Guided percutaneous needle aspiration or catheter drainage of a lung abscess â€“ Microbiologic specimens may be obtained by ultrasonography or computed tomography-guided needle aspiration or catheter drainage. Ultrasonography is preferred because of the lack of radiation exposure.

- Lung biopsy, either by a thoracoscopic or thoracotomy approach â€“ Samples obtained by lung biopsy often yield diagnostic information in children who had nondiagnostic BAL [75-77].

At least three weeks of intravenous (IV) antibiotic therapy should be delivered before lobectomy is considered for treatment failure [78]. Percutaneous drainage with catheter placement should be avoided, if possible, in children with necrotizing pneumonia. This procedure increases the risk of further complications, such as the development of bronchopleural fistulae [68,69,79,80].

# **Discharge criteria** â€” Discharge criteria for children who have been admitted to the hospital with CAP have not been standardized but typically include [1,52]:

- Vital signs have improved
- Child is able to maintain adequate fluid and nutrition orally
- Improvement in respiratory status has improved
- SpO<sub>2</sub> is â‰¥90 percent in room air
- Overall clinical status has improved, including level of activity and appetite
- Afebrile or decreased fever for at least 12 to 24 hours
- Mental status is stable and at baseline
- Caregiver is able to administer home antibiotic regimen, and child is able to comply with therapy
- Child can be discharged to a safe and compliant home environment

Outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy (OPAT) is an option for selected patients who require prolonged parenteral treatment (usually for complicated CAP that for some reason cannot be treated with an oral antibiotic) and have stabilized clinically [52,81,82]. Eligibility for OPAT requires a suitable home environment and a pharmacologic agent with a reasonable dosing schedule [83]. Decisions regarding OPAT should involve the caregivers, an infectious diseases specialist (or clinician knowledgeable about the use of antimicrobial agents in OPAT), a hospital pharmacist, and the primary care provider. The services of a visiting nurse may be required for home visits, education of caregiver(s) and observation of caregiver administration, and/or obtaining blood samples for therapeutic monitoring.

## **Follow-up and prognosis**

- **Follow-up**
  - **Primary care follow-up** â€“ Children with pneumonia should be seen by their primary care provider soon after discharge to ensure that clinical improvement continues and antibiotic therapy is being taken as prescribed without ill effects [52]. Decisions regarding the timing of primary care follow-up should involve the child's primary care provider and include the clinical status of the child at the time of discharge.
  - **Resolution of symptoms** â€“ Children who are appropriately treated for pneumonia should gradually improve with time. Cough may persist for as long as three to four months after viral pneumonia. Children who are recovering from typical or atypical bacterial pneumonia may continue to cough for several weeks and have moderate dyspnea on

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pneumonia-in-children-greater-than28-days-old-inpatient-treatment/print?search=pneumonia&source=searc... 24/57

3/18/26, 5:06 PM Pneumonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment - UpToDate

exertion for two to three months [84]. Symptomatic treatment of cough is discussed separately. (See "The common cold in children: Management and prevention", section on 'Cough'.)

- **Radiographs** â€“ Follow-up radiographs are not necessary in asymptomatic children with uncomplicated CAP, including round pneumonia [85]. However, in children with complicated pneumonia, particularly those who required invasive interventions, follow-up radiographs help to ensure resolution [2]. Follow-up radiographs may also be helpful in children with recurrent pneumonia, persistent symptoms, severe atelectasis, or unusually located infiltrates [2]. When follow-up radiographs are indicated, they should be obtained two to three weeks after hospital discharge.

Several studies have evaluated the utility of follow-up radiographs in cohorts of children with acute radiologically proven CAP [86-91]. Three of the studies included clinical as well as radiologic follow-up at three to seven weeks after initial diagnosis [86-89]. In each of these studies, follow-up radiographs were normal or improved in asymptomatic children. Residual radiographic findings, even when present, did not result in additional therapy.

Conditions that should be considered if symptoms persist in children with round pneumonia include congenital lung sequestration, pulmonary arteriovenous malformation, metastatic Wilms tumor, cavitary necrosis, pleural pseudocyst, and primary lung carcinoma [85,92-96].

- **Prognosis** â€“ Most otherwise healthy children with pneumonia recover without sequelae, even if the pneumonia is complicated [52,79,80,97]. In a multicenter cohort study, approximately 3 percent of 82,566 children hospitalized with pneumonia were readmitted with pneumonia within 30 days of discharge; 8 percent were readmitted for any reason. Readmission was more common among children younger than one year of age and children with chronic medical conditions [98].

Although some data suggest that nearly one-half of children who are hospitalized for viral pneumonia have symptoms of asthma five years after hospitalization, it is not clear whether this is related to unrecognized asthma at the time of presentation with pneumonia or a causal relationship between community-acquired viral pneumonia and development of asthma [99,100].

The overall pneumonia mortality rate in resource-abundant countries is <1 per 1000 per year [51,101]. Pneumococcal pneumonia case fatality rates (not adjusted for comorbid conditions) for children in the United States were estimated to be 4 percent in children younger than two years and 2 percent in children 2 to 17 years before the introduction of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) [102].

https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pneumonia-in-children-greater-than28-days-old-inpatient-treatment/print?search=pneumonia&source=searc... 25/57

3/18/26, 5:06 PM
Pneumonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment - UpToDate

The introduction of PCVs has resulted in a dramatic reduction (37 to 80 percent) in invasive disease and mortality rates in the countries in which they have been introduced [103]. However, pneumococcal pneumonia mortality rates have not been specifically examined. Data from the United States Pediatric Multicenter Pneumococcal Surveillance Study Group demonstrated all-cause pneumococcal mortality rates of 1 percent after the introduction of the seven-valent PCV (PCV7; during 2006 to 2009) and 0 percent after the introduction of the 13-valent PCV (PCV13; during 2011 to 2014) [104]. In a study from eastern Gambia, introduction of a nine-valent PCV was associated with a reduction in all-cause mortality from 30.1 to 25.2 per 1000 child-years [105]. (See "Pneumococcal vaccination in children", section on 'Efficacy and effectiveness'.)

- **Hospital-acquired pneumonia** â€“ For patients with hospital-acquired pneumonia, we suggest empiric treatment with piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, or cefepime (**Grade 2C**). For children in whom methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA) is suspected, we suggest the addition of vancomycin or linezolid to the regimen (**Grade 2C**). (See 'Hospital-acquired pneumonia' above.)

- **Immunocompromised host** â€“ Immunocompromised children who are hospitalized with pneumonia require broad-spectrum empiric coverage. Consultation with an infectious disease specialist is advised. (See 'Immunocompromised host' above.)

- **Pathogen-directed therapy** â€“ If microbiologic testing identifies a specific pathogen, antibiotic therapy is directed toward the specific pathogen. (See 'Pathogen-directed therapy' above.)

- **Duration of treatment** â€“ Parenteral therapy is typically transitioned to oral therapy when the patient has been afebrile for 24 to 48 hours and can tolerate oral intake. The total duration of antibiotic therapy is usually five to seven days for uncomplicated CAP. Up to four weeks of antimicrobial therapy may be necessary for complicated CAP. (See 'Duration of treatment' above.)

- **Treatment failure** â€“ The respiratory status of children receiving appropriate antimicrobial therapy for CAP should improve within 48 to 72 hours. Children who fail to improve as anticipated may not be receiving adequate antibiotic therapy, may have developed complications, or may have an alternative or coincident diagnosis. (See 'Treatment failure' above.)

- **Follow-up and prognosis** â€“ Children recovering from CAP may continue to cough for several weeks to four months, depending upon the etiology. Those recovering from typical or atypical bacterial pneumonia may also have moderate dyspnea on exertion for two to three months. After this recovery period, most otherwise healthy children do not have any long-term sequelae. (See 'Follow-up and prognosis' above.)

Follow-up radiographs are not necessary in asymptomatic children with uncomplicated CAP, including round pneumonia. However, in children with complicated pneumonia, especially those who required intervention, follow-up radiographs help to ensure resolution. (See 'Follow-up and prognosis' above.)

# **GRAPHICS**

## Table 1: **Indications for inpatient management of community-acquired pneumonia in children**

| Indication                                                            | Comment                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Most children <3 to 6 months of age                                   | Exception: a viral etiology or *Chlamydia trachomatis* is suspected \*\*and\*\* the child is relatively asymptomatic without hypoxia                                                           |
| Inability to care for at home                                         | Any child whose caregiver(s) cannot provide appropriate care or follow the management instructions                                                                                             |
| Hypoxia                                                               | SpOâ‚‚ <90% on room air                                                                                                                                                                          |
| Dehydration                                                           | Inability to maintain oral hydration or inability to feed an infant                                                                                                                            |
| Moderate to severe respiratory distress                               | Examples: RR >70 breaths per minute for infants <12 months of age, RR >50 breaths per minute for children â‰¥12 months of age, retractions, nasal flaring, difficulty breathing, apnea, grunting |
| Toxic appearance                                                      | Toxic appearance is more common in bacterial pneumonia and may suggest more severe illness                                                                                                     |
| Underlying conditions that predispose to a more severe course         | Examples: cardiopulmonary disease, genetic syndromes, neurocognitive disorders                                                                                                                 |
| Underlying conditions that may be exacerbated by pneumonia            | Example: metabolic disorder                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Underlying conditions that may adversely affect response to treatment | Example: immunocompromised host                                                                                                                                                                |
| Complications of pneumonia present                                    | Examples: effusion/empyema, necrotizing process, lung abscess                                                                                                                                  |
| Suspicion or confirmation of a pathogen that has increased virulence  | Examples: *Staphylococcus aureus*, group A *Streptococcus*                                                                                                                                     |
| Failure of outpatient therapy                                         | Continued lack of response within 48 to 72 hours of antibiotic change                                                                                                                          |

We recommend that children with any of the above indications be hospitalized for management of CAP.

**CAP:** community-acquired pneumonia; RR: respiratory rate; SpO<sub>2</sub>: peripheral capillary oxygen saturation.
